title: Antibodies, allergies and HIV: how the defence remembers, and three ways it goes wrong

summary.text: A doctor can take one drop of your blood and tell which germs you met years ago. How can blood hold a record? In this lesson you will run a colour test on three pretend patients to measure how much antibody each one has, and find out why a test can miss a new infection. You will stroke your arm to wake the cells that cause allergies, count who lived and died in Boston in 1721, and model what HIV does to helper T cells. You will also learn why the defence sometimes attacks harmless food, or the body itself.
summary.art: A girl holding up a white ice tray in which the wells run from deep red at one end to yellow at the other, with a jar of turmeric and a tumbler of water beside her on a kitchen counter.

intro.hook: A mosquito bites you and flies away. Ten minutes later a bump rises and itches. The mosquito has gone, so who made the bump?
intro.text: Your own body made the bump. A mosquito leaves a little saliva in your skin. Your immune system has met that saliva before, and it has made antibodies against it. Antibodies are tiny Y-shaped proteins that fit one target and nothing else. The bump and the itch are your body answering the saliva. A baby who is bitten for the very first time usually gets no bump at all, because the baby's body has no record of mosquito saliva yet. So a bump is a sign that your body remembers. In this lesson you will find out how the body keeps that record, how doctors read it, and what happens when the defence answers the wrong thing.
intro.art: A close view of a child's forearm with one small round mosquito bump, and the child looking at it with a magnifying glass while a mosquito flies off through the window.

outcomes: I can describe the shape of an antibody and name three things antibodies do to a germ.
I can explain how plasma cells and memory cells keep a record of a germ for many years.
I can explain how a blood test finds antibodies, and why the test can miss a new infection.
I can explain what happens in the body in an allergy, and what to do in a serious one.
I can explain how the body learns not to attack itself, and what an autoimmune disease is.
I can explain how HIV harms the immune system, how medicines hold HIV back, and how HIV does and does not spread.
I can tell how Onesimus, the tikadars of India and Edward Jenner protected people from smallpox.
I can use the numbers from a test or a count to compare two things fairly.

terms.meaning: An antigen is any molecule that the immune system can recognise by its shape. Most antigens are proteins or sugars on the outside of a germ.
terms.example: The spike on the outside of a measles virus is an antigen. So is a protein in mosquito saliva.
terms.art: A round virus with small spikes on the outside, and one spike drawn larger in a circle beside them with the label antigen.

terms.meaning: An antibody is a Y-shaped protein made by the immune system. The two tips of the Y are the same, and they fit one antigen.
terms.example: An antibody against measles sticks to a measles virus. The same antibody does not stick to a chickenpox virus.
terms.art: A Y-shaped antibody with its two tips coloured, each tip touching a matching bump on a round germ.

terms.meaning: Immunoglobulin is the scientists' name for an antibody. It is shortened to Ig. Humans make five classes: IgM, IgG, IgA, IgE and IgD.
terms.example: IgG is the main antibody in blood. IgA is the main antibody in tears, spit and mother's milk.
terms.art: Five small antibody drawings in a row, labelled IgM, IgG, IgA, IgE and IgD, with IgM drawn as five Y shapes joined in a ring.

terms.meaning: A B cell is a white blood cell that carries one kind of antibody on their surface. When that antibody meets a matching antigen, the B cell divides into many cells.
terms.example: A B cell whose antibody fits tetanus toxin rests in a lymph node until that toxin arrives.
terms.art: A round white blood cell with many small Y shapes sticking out of the surface like pins in a pincushion.

terms.meaning: A plasma cell is a B cell who has changed into an antibody factory. One plasma cell can release thousands of antibodies every second.
terms.example: Plasma cells living in your bone marrow still release measles antibodies years after your measles vaccine.
terms.art: An egg-shaped cell with a large busy inside, releasing a stream of tiny Y shapes into a blood vessel.

terms.meaning: A memory cell is a B cell or T cell who stays alive for years after an infection. Memory cells divide fast if the same antigen comes back.
terms.example: People who lived through the flu of 1918 still had memory B cells against that virus ninety years later.
terms.art: A small quiet white blood cell resting inside a lymph node, with a tiny calendar showing many years beside the cell.

terms.meaning: Clumping is what happens when antibodies join many germs into one lump. It works because each antibody has two arms and can hold two germs. Scientists call it agglutination.
terms.example: Germs in a clump cannot spread out, and one phagocyte can swallow the whole clump.
terms.art: Six round germs joined into one lump by Y-shaped antibodies, each antibody holding one germ with each arm.

terms.meaning: A titre is a measure of how much antibody a sample holds. You dilute the sample step by step. The titre is the weakest dilution that still tests positive.
terms.example: If a blood sample still tests positive when it is 64 times weaker, but not at 256 times weaker, the titre is 64.
terms.art: A row of five small bowls of liquid, the first three red and the last two yellow, with an arrow pointing at the third bowl.

terms.meaning: The window period is the time just after an infection when a test still says no. The germ is in the body, but there is not yet enough antibody for the test to find.
terms.example: A person tested for HIV too soon after catching the virus can get a negative result, so the test is repeated later.
terms.art: A calendar of several weeks with a small virus on day one, a rising line of Y shapes, and a test strip that turns positive only in the last weeks.

terms.meaning: An allergy is an immune response against something harmless, such as pollen, dust mites or a food. The response itself causes the trouble.
terms.example: A child with a peanut allergy may get itchy lips and a rash within minutes of eating one peanut.
terms.art: A child sneezing beside a flowering tree, with tiny yellow pollen grains drifting in the air.

terms.meaning: An allergen is the harmless thing that sets off an allergy. It is an antigen that the body answers with IgE antibodies.
terms.example: Common allergens in India are house dust mites, pollen, cockroach droppings, milk, egg, peanuts and prawns.
terms.art: A tray holding a peanut, a glass of milk, a prawn, an egg and a magnified dust mite, each with a small warning triangle.

terms.meaning: IgE is the class of antibody that causes allergies. IgE antibodies sit on mast cells and wait. Blood holds less IgE than any other class of antibody.
terms.example: A person who is allergic to prawns has IgE antibodies that fit a prawn protein.
terms.art: A mast cell with many small Y shapes standing on the surface, their two arms pointing outward.

terms.meaning: A mast cell is an immune cell who lives in the skin, the nose, the lungs and the gut. Mast cells are packed with tiny bags of histamine.
terms.example: Mast cells in your skin release histamine around a mosquito bite, and a bump rises.
terms.art: A round cell under the skin filled with dark dots, some of the dots spilling out towards a nearby blood vessel.

terms.meaning: Histamine is a chemical that mast cells release. It widens small blood vessels and makes them leaky, and it makes nerve endings itch.
terms.example: Medicines for hay fever are called antihistamines, because they stop histamine from acting on cells.
terms.art: Small dots leaving a mast cell and reaching a blood vessel that is swelling wider, with fluid leaking out into the skin.

terms.meaning: Anaphylaxis is a severe allergic reaction all over the body. Histamine is released in many places at once. Breathing becomes hard and blood pressure falls. It is an emergency.
terms.example: A person in anaphylaxis needs an injection of adrenaline and a hospital straight away.
terms.art: A grown-up holding an adrenaline injector pen against the outer thigh of a child who is sitting down, with a phone showing an ambulance number.

terms.meaning: The thymus is a soft organ behind the breastbone, above the heart. Young T cells are tested there. The T cells who would attack the body's own cells are removed.
terms.example: A child's thymus is large and busy. A grown-up's thymus has shrunk and is mostly fat.
terms.art: A child's chest seen from the front with a soft two-lobed organ drawn above the heart, behind the breastbone.

terms.meaning: Tolerance means that the immune system does not attack a certain antigen. The body is tolerant of its own cells, of food and of friendly microbes.
terms.example: You eat rice every day and your immune system does not attack rice proteins. That is tolerance.
terms.art: A white blood cell passing calmly by a plate of rice, a red blood cell and a friendly gut microbe.

terms.meaning: An autoimmune disease is an illness in which the immune system attacks some of the body's own cells. 'Auto' means self.
terms.example: In type 1 diabetes, T cells destroy the cells in the pancreas who make insulin.
terms.art: A group of white blood cells crowding round a small cluster of the body's own cells in the pancreas.

terms.meaning: A helper T cell is a white blood cell who switches other immune cells on. Helper T cells tell B cells to make antibodies. They are also called CD4 cells.
terms.example: Without a signal from a helper T cell, most B cells do not become plasma cells.
terms.art: One white blood cell touching a B cell and passing small signal dots across, while the B cell begins to divide.

terms.meaning: HIV is a virus who infects helper T cells and destroys them over years. The letters stand for human immunodeficiency virus.
terms.example: HIV passes from person to person in blood, in sex between grown-ups, and from a mother to her baby.
terms.art: A small round virus with knobs on the surface, with one knob fitting a matching knob on a much larger helper T cell.

terms.meaning: AIDS is the illness that follows when HIV has destroyed most of a person's helper T cells. Germs that a healthy body controls easily can then cause serious disease.
terms.example: A person with HIV who takes medicine every day may never get AIDS.
terms.art: A line graph that falls slowly over many years, with a dotted line near the bottom marked 200.

terms.meaning: Antiretroviral medicines stop HIV from copying themselves inside cells. A person takes them every day for life. The treatment is shortened to ART.
terms.example: In India, government ART centres give these medicines free.
terms.art: A hand holding a small strip of tablets beside a calendar with every day ticked.

terms.meaning: Inoculation was an old way of protecting people from smallpox. A little matter from a smallpox blister was put into a scratch on a healthy person. It is also called variolation.
terms.example: Onesimus was inoculated as a boy in West Africa. In Bengal, people called tikadars did the same work.
terms.art: A hand making a small scratch on a child's upper arm with a needle, with a small pot beside it, in a scene from three hundred years ago.

explanations.concept: An antibody is a Y-shaped protein with two arms
explanations.definition: An antibody is a protein shaped like the letter Y. The two tips of the Y are exactly alike, and each tip fits one antigen.
explanations.description: An antibody is built from four chains of protein, two long and two short, held together in a Y. It is about ten nanometres long. A million antibodies laid end to end would be about one centimetre. The stem of the Y is nearly the same in every antibody of one class. The tips differ from one B cell's antibody to the next, and the tips are where the antibody fits its antigen. Why two tips and not one? With two tips, one antibody can hold two germs at once, or hold one germ in two places. Holding in two places is much firmer than holding in one. Nobody shapes a tip to suit a germ. The tips are made before any germ arrives. A tip fits an antigen because their shapes and electric charges match closely, the way your hand fits a glove made for it. Rodney Porter in England and Gerald Edelman in the United States worked out this structure around 1960. They shared the Nobel Prize for it in 1972.
examples: An antibody against tetanus toxin holds a toxin molecule at each tip.
An antibody against a measles virus does not stick to a chickenpox virus, because the shapes do not match.
IgM, the first antibody made in an infection, is five Y shapes joined in a ring, so it has ten tips.
explanations.art: A large Y-shaped antibody drawn as four chains, two long and two short, with the two tips coloured and a small scale bar marked ten nanometres.

explanations.concept: What antibodies do to a germ: block, clump and flag
explanations.definition: Antibodies do not kill a germ by themselves. They block the germ, join germs into clumps, and flag them so that other parts of the defence destroy them.
explanations.description: Many people picture antibodies as tiny weapons. That is not correct. An antibody is a sticker with two sticky tips. It helps in three main ways. First, blocking. A virus gets into a cell by fitting part of their surface to a part of the cell. If antibodies cover that part, the virus cannot get in. A toxin, which is a poison made by a germ, is blocked in the same way. Second, clumping. Each antibody can hold two germs, so many antibodies tie many germs into one lump. A lump cannot spread through the body, and one phagocyte can swallow the whole of it. A phagocyte is a white blood cell who swallows germs. Third, flagging. Phagocytes have grips that fit the stem of the Y. A germ coated in antibodies is caught and swallowed far more quickly than a bare germ. Antibodies on a bacterium also switch on complement. Complement is a set of blood proteins that make holes in the outer skin of bacteria.
examples: Antibodies against the diphtheria toxin block the toxin before it reaches your cells.
When a doctor checks a blood group, antibodies clump red blood cells of the wrong group, and the clumps are easy to see.
A bacterium coated in antibodies is swallowed by a phagocyte within minutes.
explanations.art: Three small panels: antibodies covering the spikes of a virus at a cell's surface, antibodies tying several bacteria into a lump, and a phagocyte gripping the stems of antibodies on a coated bacterium.

explanations.concept: Plasma cells and memory cells: how the record is kept
explanations.definition: After an infection, some B cells become plasma cells who go on releasing antibodies, and others become memory cells who wait. Together they are the body's record of that germ.
explanations.description: When a B cell's antibody fits an antigen, and a helper T cell gives the signal, the B cell divides. Most of the new cells become plasma cells. A plasma cell is a factory that releases thousands of antibodies every second. Most plasma cells die within days or weeks. Some travel to the bone marrow, the soft inside of your bones, and live there for years. Here is a puzzle. One IgG antibody lasts only about three weeks in the blood before the body breaks it down. Yet people still have measles antibodies fifty years after measles. How? The long-lived plasma cells in the bone marrow keep making fresh ones, year after year. In 2007, scientists in the United States reported on blood samples saved from 45 people over many years. The level of measles antibody had hardly fallen. Tetanus antibody fell faster, by half in about eleven years, which is one reason tetanus needs boosters. Memory cells are the second half of the record. They make no antibody while they wait. If the germ returns, they divide at once into new plasma cells.
examples: Old people who lived through the 1918 flu still had memory B cells against that virus about ninety years later.
A tetanus booster is given because the level of tetanus antibody slowly falls.
Your bone marrow holds plasma cells for many different germs and vaccines at the same time.
explanations.art: A cut-open bone showing the marrow, with a few egg-shaped plasma cells releasing streams of tiny Y shapes into a blood vessel, and a small calendar marked with many years.

explanations.concept: Reading the record: how an antibody test works, and when it misses
explanations.definition: An antibody test does not look for the germ. It looks for antibodies against the germ in a person's blood. It can miss an infection that is only a few weeks old.
explanations.description: Many blood tests for infections look for antibodies. The test has pieces of the germ fixed to a plate or a strip. A drop of the person's blood serum is added. Serum is the clear yellowish liquid part of blood. If the serum holds antibodies that fit, they stick. A second chemical then makes a colour appear. Colour means that antibodies are there. To measure how much antibody there is, the serum is diluted step by step, and each step is tested. The weakest dilution that still gives colour is called the titre. A high titre means a lot of antibody. This kind of test has a weakness. After a first infection, the body needs time to make antibodies. For one to three weeks there are too few to find. With HIV, most tests cannot find antibodies until some weeks after infection, and a few people take up to three months. This gap is called the window period. A person in the window period has the virus and can pass them on, but the test says no. That is why a test is repeated later. A test that looks for the germ's own genes can find an infection sooner.
examples: The ELISA test that found the first HIV cases in India in 1986 showed a yellow colour where antibodies were present.
Before a child gets some vaccines again, a doctor can measure the titre to see whether the first dose still protects.
Blood banks in India test every lesson of donated blood for HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C.
explanations.art: A white plastic plate with rows of small wells, some wells yellow and some clear, with a gloved hand adding a drop to one well from a thin dropper.

explanations.concept: Five classes of antibody for five kinds of job
explanations.definition: Humans make five classes of antibody, called IgM, IgG, IgA, IgE and IgD. The tips can be the same while the stem differs, and the stem decides where the antibody goes and what happens next.
explanations.description: Why does one body need five classes? The tips of the Y decide what the antibody sticks to. The stem decides what happens after that. So a B cell can keep the same tips and change the stem, to send the same fit to a different place. IgM comes first in a new infection. It is five Y shapes joined in a ring. Each tip of a new antibody holds weakly, so ten tips together make up for that. IgG comes next. It is the main antibody in blood and it lasts longest. In a pregnant mother, IgG passes across the placenta into the baby's blood. So a newborn has a copy of the mother's record for the first months. IgA is released into tears, spit, the lining of the nose and gut, and mother's milk. It meets germs before they get inside. IgE sits on mast cells and is the antibody of allergies. IgD is found on the surface of young B cells. Scientists are still not sure of all that IgD does.
examples: A baby drinking mother's milk swallows IgA, which coats the inside of the baby's gut.
A test that finds IgM against dengue virus points to a recent infection. IgG alone points to an older one.
A person with hay fever has IgE that fits a pollen protein.
explanations.art: A body outline with five small antibody shapes placed where each works: IgM and IgG in a blood vessel, IgA in tears and the gut, IgE on a mast cell in the skin, and IgD on a B cell.

explanations.concept: Allergy: a full alarm for a harmless thing
explanations.definition: In an allergy, the body makes IgE antibodies against something harmless. When that thing comes again, mast cells release histamine, and the histamine causes the itching, swelling and sneezing.
explanations.description: An allergy needs two meetings. At the first meeting nothing seems to happen. But some B cells make IgE that fits the allergen, perhaps a protein in peanut. The IgE antibodies fix their stems to mast cells in the skin, nose, lungs and gut, with the tips pointing outward. Now the person is ready to react. At the next meeting, one allergen molecule touches the tips of two IgE antibodies on the same mast cell and links them. Within a minute or two the mast cell releases bags of histamine. Histamine widens small blood vessels and makes them leaky, so fluid moves out into the skin or the lining of the nose. That gives a rash, a runny nose, watery eyes and swelling. Histamine also makes nerve endings itch. In the lungs it tightens the airways. A mosquito bump is a small, safe allergic reaction to mosquito saliva. A severe reaction all over the body is called anaphylaxis. The throat can swell, breathing becomes hard and blood pressure falls. It needs an injection of adrenaline and an ambulance at once. In India the ambulance number is 108, and the emergency number is 112.
examples: A baby bitten by a mosquito for the first time usually gets no bump, because the baby has no IgE against the saliva yet.
A child allergic to house dust mites sneezes when old bedding is shaken.
Antihistamine tablets work by stopping histamine from acting on cells.
explanations.art: Two panels: first, a mast cell with IgE antibodies standing on the surface. Second, a peanut protein linking two of the antibodies while dark dots of histamine burst out of the cell.

explanations.concept: Why do allergies exist at all?
explanations.description: IgE and mast cells cost the body energy to make, and they can kill. So why do we have them? Scientists have several ideas, and each has some evidence. Nobody has settled the question. Allergies have also become more common in many countries in the last sixty years, in rich countries first and now in many cities of Asia. Human genes cannot change that fast, so something in the way people live must have changed. The ideas below are not rivals in every way. More than one may be true.
examples: In 2013, two teams found that mice who had met bee venom once made IgE against the venom. Those mice survived a larger dose later, and mice with no IgE did not.
Later mouse studies found the same for the venom of Russell's viper, a snake found across India.

In a British study published in 2015, babies at high risk of peanut allergy either ate peanut foods from their first year or avoided peanut. By age five, about 17 in 100 of the avoiders were allergic, and about 3 in 100 of the eaters.

perspectives.explanation: IgE and mast cells fight parasitic worms, who are too big for a phagocyte to swallow. Itching, sneezing, mucus and a rushing gut help to push a worm out. Where worms are rare, the same system fires at pollen and food instead.

perspectives.who: The toxin idea, from Margie Profet in 1991
perspectives.explanation: Allergic reactions are a defence against poisons such as venoms and harmful plant chemicals. Sneezing, vomiting and scratching get a poison out of the body fast. The mouse studies of 2013 support this for bee and snake venom.

A young immune system needs to meet many harmless microbes from soil, animals and other children. They teach it what to ignore. With fewer of these meetings, it learns less well. David Strachan first suggested something like this in 1989.

The gut teaches tolerance. A baby who eats a food early learns to tolerate it. A baby who first meets the food through sore, broken skin may make IgE against that food. The 2015 peanut study supports this.

explanations.art: A mast cell in the middle with four arrows pointing out to a parasitic worm, a bee and a snake, a child playing in soil with a dog, and a baby being fed a spoon of peanut paste.

explanations.concept: Telling self from not-self: the test in the thymus
explanations.definition: Tolerance means that the immune system does not attack the body's own cells. Much of it is learned in the thymus, where T cells who would attack the body are removed before they are let out.
explanations.description: B cells and T cells get their receptors by a shuffle of genes, with no plan. A receptor is the part of a cell that fits an antigen. A random shuffle must also make some receptors that fit the body's own molecules. Those cells would be dangerous. So young T cells are tested in the thymus, a soft organ behind the breastbone. Cells of the thymus show the young T cells samples of the body's own proteins, even proteins that belong to the eye or the pancreas. A T cell whose receptor grips one of these strongly is given a signal to die. A T cell whose receptor is of no use at all dies too. In mice, about 95 out of every 100 young T cells die in the thymus and never leave. Jacques Miller found out what the thymus is for in 1961. He removed the thymus from newborn mice, and they grew up with almost no defence. The test is not perfect. So a second guard exists outside the thymus. Regulatory T cells are T cells who calm other immune cells down. Shimon Sakaguchi found them in 1995, and Mary Brunkow and Fred Ramsdell found the gene they depend on. The three shared the Nobel Prize in 2025.
examples: Your immune system leaves your own red blood cells alone but attacks red blood cells of the wrong blood group.
A child's thymus is large. It shrinks from the teenage years, because most of the testing is done early in life.
Babies born without a working thymus have very few T cells and catch many infections.
explanations.art: A cutaway of the thymus as a room where small young T cells file past large cells holding up samples, with most of the T cells fading away and a few leaving through a door into a blood vessel.

explanations.concept: Autoimmune disease: the defence attacks the body
explanations.definition: An autoimmune disease is an illness in which a person's own immune system attacks some of their own cells. Tolerance has failed for one part of the body.
explanations.description: In each autoimmune disease, the target is different. In type 1 diabetes, T cells destroy the cells of the pancreas who make insulin. The child must then take insulin every day. In Hashimoto's disease, antibodies and T cells attack the thyroid gland in the neck. In rheumatoid arthritis the joints are attacked, and they swell and hurt. In coeliac disease, gluten, a protein in wheat, sets off an attack on the person's own gut lining. In vitiligo, patches of skin turn white. Most scientists think this is the immune system destroying the cells who make skin colour. Why does tolerance fail? Genes matter. So do triggers such as certain infections. Sometimes a germ's antigen looks so much like a body molecule that the antibodies made against the germ fit the body too. In rheumatic fever, antibodies made against a throat bacterium also stick to the heart. About four out of five people with autoimmune diseases are women, and nobody is sure why. Autoimmune diseases are not catching. They are treated with medicines that replace what was lost, or that calm the immune system. Most cannot yet be cured.
examples: A child with type 1 diabetes checks blood sugar and takes insulin before meals.
A person with coeliac disease stays well by eating no wheat, barley or rye. Rice, ragi, jowar and bajra are safe.
Vitiligo is not catching. You cannot get it by touching someone.
explanations.art: A body outline with four places marked: the thyroid in the neck, the pancreas, the gut lining and the joints of a hand, each with a few white blood cells crowding round the body's own cells.

explanations.concept: HIV: a virus who infects the helper T cells
explanations.definition: HIV is a virus who enters helper T cells, copies themselves there and destroys those cells over years. With too few helper T cells, the rest of the defence does not get switched on.
explanations.description: A virus must get inside a cell to copy themselves. Each kind of virus fits certain cells. HIV fits a molecule called CD4, which sits on helper T cells. That is the worst possible cell to lose. Helper T cells give the signal that lets B cells make antibodies and lets killer T cells work. HIV carries their genes as RNA. Inside the cell, an enzyme copies the RNA into DNA, and the DNA is joined into the cell's own DNA. From then on the cell makes new viruses. This copying makes many mistakes, so HIV changes very fast. Antibodies made against last month's virus fit this month's virus poorly. A healthy person has roughly 500 to 1,500 helper T cells in a cubic millimetre of blood, a drop the size of a pinhead. Without treatment the number falls slowly for about ten years on average. The person feels well for most of that time. Below 200, germs that a healthy body controls easily cause serious illness. That stage is called AIDS. Tuberculosis is the most common killer of people with AIDS. Françoise Barré-Sinoussi and Luc Montagnier in Paris found the virus in 1983.
examples: A person can carry HIV for years, look healthy and not know, which is why testing matters.
The fungus that causes thrush is kept in check in a healthy mouth. In a person with AIDS the fungus can spread down the throat.
The body does make antibodies against HIV. That is how the test works. But the virus changes too fast for them to clear the infection.
explanations.art: A round virus with knobs fitting onto a matching knob on a large helper T cell, and beside it the same cell later releasing many small new viruses.

explanations.concept: Living with HIV: medicines, and how HIV does and does not spread
explanations.definition: Antiretroviral medicines stop HIV from copying. A person who takes them every day can live a long and healthy life, and when the virus in their blood is too low to measure they do not pass HIV on through sex.
explanations.description: HIV passes from one person to another in only a few ways. The virus travels in blood, in the body fluids shared in sex between grown-ups, and from a mother to her baby during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding. HIV does not pass through hugging, shaking hands, sharing a plate or a tumbler, coughing, toilets, swimming pools or mosquitoes. You can play, eat and study with a person who has HIV with no risk at all. Since 1996, doctors have given three antiretroviral medicines together. Why three? HIV changes so fast that a virus able to resist one medicine soon appears. A virus who can resist three at once is very unlikely. The medicines do not remove the virus. HIV DNA stays hidden inside resting cells, and the virus returns if the medicines stop. So they are taken for life. In 2001 these medicines cost more than 10,000 dollars a year for one person. That year Yusuf Hamied of the Indian company Cipla offered them at 350 dollars a year, less than a dollar a day. Millions of people in Africa and Asia could then be treated. India has given the medicines free since 2004. A mother on treatment has a very small chance of passing HIV to her baby.
examples: In 2023, about 25 lakh people in India were living with HIV.
Hospitals use a new sterile needle for every injection, so that no blood passes between patients.
A pregnant woman in India is offered an HIV test, so that treatment can protect her baby.
explanations.art: Two children sharing a tiffin box and laughing in a school yard, with small ticks beside drawings of a hug, a shared tumbler and a mosquito.

explanations.concept: Onesimus, the tikadars and Jenner: protection before anyone knew of antibodies
explanations.definition: Inoculation meant putting a little matter from a smallpox blister into a scratch on a healthy person. The person usually had a mild illness and was then protected for life. People in Africa, India, China and Turkey did this long before Europe did.
explanations.description: Smallpox once killed about three in every ten people who caught the disease. People noticed that nobody caught smallpox twice. So in several parts of the world, healers gave people a small dose on purpose. In Bengal, travelling inoculators did this work. They were later known as tikadars, from tika, a mark. A British doctor, John Holwell, described their method in a report in 1767. Historians still argue about how old the practice was in India. In West Africa the practice was common too. A West African man was enslaved and taken to Boston, in America, where he was given the name Onesimus. Around 1716 he told the man who held him, a minister called Cotton Mather, that he had been inoculated as a boy and showed the scar. When smallpox struck Boston in 1721, Mather urged the town's doctors to try it. Only one, Zabdiel Boylston, agreed. He counted his results, and far fewer of the inoculated died. But inoculation used real smallpox. A few people died of it, and they could infect others. In 1796 the English doctor Edward Jenner tested a safer way, using cowpox, a mild disease caught from cows. That was the first vaccine. In 1980 the World Health Organization declared that smallpox was gone from the Earth. Nobody in this story knew that antibodies and memory cells existed. They knew what worked.
examples: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu saw inoculation in Turkey and had her daughter inoculated in London in 1721.
Jenner's word 'vaccine' comes from vacca, the Latin word for cow.
We do not know what name Onesimus was given by his parents, because nobody wrote it down.
explanations.art: A map of the world with four places marked, West Africa, Bengal, Boston and Gloucestershire in England, joined by dotted lines, with a small scratched arm drawn at each.

explanations.concept: Down to the atoms: why an antibody sticks
explanations.definition: An antibody holds an antigen by many weak attractions between atoms at the same time. No strong chemical bond is made, so the hold depends on a close fit.
explanations.description: Zoom in on one tip of an antibody. It is a small pocket or surface made of a few dozen amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. Some of their atoms carry a little positive electric charge, and some a little negative charge. Some parts mix well with water, and some avoid it. An antigen sticks when its bumps sit in the hollows of the tip, and its positive spots lie against negative spots. Each single attraction is very weak. The moving water around them could break it at once. But when many weak attractions act together, the antigen stays. This is why shape matters so much. A molecule that is slightly the wrong shape touches at only a few points and drifts away. It is also why an antibody can let go. Heat, acid or strong salt loosens the hold. Weak attractions of this kind also hold a gecko's foot to a wall. So the whole of antibody recognition comes down to atoms attracting and repelling each other by their charges.
examples: During an infection, B cells whose antibodies hold more firmly are chosen again and again, so later antibodies fit better than early ones.
A penicillin molecule is too small to act as an antigen alone. Joined to a body protein it can become one, and a few people become allergic.
Scientists now design antibodies as medicines. Their names often end in 'mab'.
explanations.art: A close view of the tip of an antibody as a bumpy pocket with small plus and minus signs, and an antigen with matching bumps and opposite signs sitting in the pocket.

explanations.description: Much about this defence is still unknown. Nobody has made a vaccine that protects well against HIV, after more than forty years of trying. The virus changes too fast, and hides inside the DNA of resting cells. A very small number of people have been cured of HIV. The first was Timothy Ray Brown, who was treated in Berlin in 2007. He had a blood cancer, and he was given new bone marrow from a donor whose cells lack a doorway that HIV uses. This treatment is far too dangerous to give to people who are not already very ill. Nobody knows why most people with autoimmune diseases are women. Nobody knows exactly why allergies have become more common, or why one child outgrows a milk allergy and another does not. Nobody knows how some plasma cells stay alive for a lifetime while others die in a week. These are open questions that scientists are working on now.
examples: A few people control HIV for many years without medicine. Scientists study them to learn how.
Children often outgrow allergies to milk and egg, but much less often an allergy to peanuts.
New medicines for some autoimmune diseases calm one part of the immune system and leave the rest working.

perspectives.who: Scientists working on an HIV vaccine
perspectives.explanation: Some think a vaccine must teach the body to make rare antibodies that fit the parts of HIV that cannot change. Others think it must train T cells instead. Neither has worked well enough yet.

explanations.art: A scientist in a lab coat looking at a wall of question marks, with drawings of a virus, a thyroid gland and a peanut among them.

agreed.text: An antibody is a Y-shaped protein with two matching tips, and each tip fits one antigen.
agreed.evidence: Rodney Porter cut antibodies into three pieces with an enzyme in 1959. Two pieces still held the antigen and one did not. Later, pictures made with X-rays and electron microscopes showed the Y shape directly.

agreed.text: Antibodies do not kill germs alone. They block them, clump them and flag them for other parts of the defence.
agreed.evidence: Under a microscope, bacteria mixed with matching antibodies gather into clumps but stay alive. Add phagocytes or complement from fresh blood, and the bacteria are destroyed.

agreed.text: The body keeps making antibodies against a germ for many years after the germ has gone.
agreed.evidence: In a 2007 study, blood saved from 45 people over about fifteen years showed that the level of measles antibody hardly fell. One antibody molecule lasts only weeks, so cells must keep making new ones.

agreed.text: An allergic reaction is caused by IgE antibodies on mast cells, which release histamine when the allergen links two IgE antibodies.
agreed.evidence: Teruko and Kimishige Ishizaka found IgE in 1966, and Gunnar Johansson and Hans Bennich found it separately in Sweden. Serum from an allergic person, put into the skin of a person who is not allergic, makes that patch of skin react to the allergen.

agreed.text: The immune system can attack the body's own cells, and this causes autoimmune diseases.
agreed.evidence: In 1956, Noel Rose and Ernest Witebsky made rabbits attack their own thyroid glands. In the same year Deborah Doniach, Ivan Roitt and Peter Campbell found antibodies against the thyroid in the blood of patients with Hashimoto's disease.

agreed.text: HIV causes AIDS by destroying helper T cells, and antiretroviral medicines stop the virus from copying.
agreed.evidence: The virus was found in 1983 in patients' lymph nodes. The number of helper T cells in the blood falls as the amount of virus rises. When people take the medicines, the virus in the blood falls and the helper T cells rise again.

agreed.text: A person with HIV whose virus is too low to measure does not pass HIV on through sex.
agreed.evidence: Large studies followed thousands of couples in which one partner had HIV and took medicine, and the other did not have HIV. Over several years, not one partner caught HIV from a person whose virus was too low to measure.

challenging.who: Many school books and news reports
challenging.for: People with plenty of antibody against a germ usually do not fall ill from that germ. So the antibodies seem to kill.
challenging.against: An antibody is only a protein that sticks. Bacteria coated in antibody stay alive in a dish. They die when a phagocyte swallows them or complement makes holes in them. Antibodies block, clump and flag.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that antibodies are weapons that kill germs.

challenging.claim: The body will never attack itself.
challenging.for: Ehrlich injected goats with the blood of other goats, and they made antibodies. Injected with their own blood, they made none. He called the idea of self-attack 'horror autotoxicus', the dread of poisoning oneself.
challenging.against: In 1956, rabbits were made to attack their own thyroid, and patients with Hashimoto's disease were found to carry antibodies against their own thyroid. Today more than eighty autoimmune diseases are known.
challenging.context: This card is about an old belief: that a body's defence cannot turn on the body's own cells.

challenging.claim: A negative test means the person is not infected.
challenging.for: Modern tests are very good. Once antibodies have appeared, an HIV antibody test finds almost every infected person.
challenging.against: An antibody test looks for the body's answer, and the answer takes weeks to appear. In the window period the virus is present and the test says no. A second test some weeks later settles it.
challenging.context: This card is about what a blood test can and cannot tell you just after an infection.

challenging.claim: Edward Jenner was the first person to protect people from smallpox.
challenging.for: Jenner tested cowpox in 1796, published his results and made a much safer method that the whole world took up.
challenging.against: People in West Africa, India, China and Turkey had inoculated against smallpox for a long time before him. Onesimus brought the knowledge to Boston about eighty years before Jenner's test. Jenner himself was inoculated as a boy.
challenging.context: This card is about who deserves credit for protecting people from smallpox.

challenging.claim: An allergy is nothing but a useless mistake of the immune system.
challenging.who: The usual view in medicine for most of the last century
challenging.for: Pollen and peanuts do no harm, yet the reaction to them can kill. Nothing seems to be gained.
challenging.against: Mice who had met bee venom once made IgE against it and survived a bigger dose later. So the allergic reaction may be a real defence against venoms and poisons, which fires at the wrong targets today.
challenging.context: This card is about whether allergic reactions have any use.

challenging.claim: You can catch HIV from a hug, a shared plate or a mosquito bite.
challenging.who: A fear held by many people in every country
challenging.for: Many illnesses do spread by touch, food or mosquitoes, so the fear seems sensible.
challenging.against: HIV breaks down quickly outside the body and does not pass through skin. A mosquito injects saliva and not the last person's blood, and HIV cannot copy inside a mosquito. Forty years of records show no case from hugging, sharing food or mosquitoes.
challenging.context: This card is about how HIV does and does not pass from one person to another.

challenging.claim: The stronger the immune system, the better.
challenging.who: Advertisements for health drinks and pills
challenging.for: People whose defence is too weak, as in AIDS, fall ill from germs that others control easily.
challenging.against: In an allergy and in an autoimmune disease the defence is too active, or aimed at the wrong thing. Doctors treat these by calming it. A healthy immune system is well aimed and well controlled, which is different from strong.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that an immune system should be made as strong as possible.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that the body's defence can attack the body? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: Around 1900 the German scientist Paul Ehrlich injected goats with blood from other goats. The goats made antibodies against it. When he injected a goat with her own blood, she made none. Ehrlich decided that a body would never attack itself. He gave the idea a Latin name, horror autotoxicus. For fifty years most doctors believed him, and few looked for diseases of self-attack. In the 1950s, in Buffalo in the United States, a young researcher called Noel Rose injected rabbits with material from their own thyroid glands, mixed with a substance that alerts the immune system. The rabbits made antibodies against their own thyroids, and the glands were damaged. His professor, Ernest Witebsky, had been taught in Ehrlich's tradition and did not believe it at first. They repeated the work and published it in 1956. In London that same year, Deborah Doniach, Ivan Roitt and Peter Campbell tested blood from patients with Hashimoto's disease, in which the thyroid slowly fails. The blood held antibodies against the patients' own thyroid. The body can attack itself.
how_we_found_out.who: Paul Ehrlich, who said the body never attacks itself. Noel Rose and Ernest Witebsky in Buffalo, and Deborah Doniach, Ivan Roitt and Peter Campbell in London, who showed that it can.
how_we_found_out.when: About 1900 (Ehrlich's idea) and 1956 (the rabbit experiments and the patients with Hashimoto's disease)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a body's immune system will never attack the body's own cells. In 1956, rabbits and human patients were both shown to make antibodies against their own thyroid glands.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman scientist in a 1950s laboratory holding up a small glass tube in which a cloudy band has formed, with a drawing of a butterfly-shaped thyroid gland pinned to the wall behind her.

big_questions.q: A test finds antibodies and never sees the germ. When is a sign of a thing as good as the thing itself?
big_questions.hint: Think of a footprint, smoke, or a cough. When could each one mislead you? What is the window period for a footprint?

big_questions.q: Your immune system leaves your gut microbes, your food and an unborn baby alone. None of them is you. So what does it count as 'self'?
big_questions.hint: Is 'self' the same as 'made of my cells'? Or is it closer to 'what I have learned to live with'?

big_questions.q: Is an allergy a mistake, or a real defence used in the wrong place?
big_questions.hint: Think about the bee venom mice. Could the same reaction be useful in one place and harmful in another?

big_questions.q: Onesimus knew how to stop smallpox. Most doctors in Boston would not listen to him. What makes people believe or doubt a piece of knowledge?
big_questions.hint: Did the doctors test what he said, or did they judge who was saying it? What should count as a good reason to believe something?

big_questions.q: The same medicines cost 10,000 dollars a year, and then 350. What should decide who gets a medicine?
big_questions.hint: Who paid for the research? Who was dying? Think about what a company needs and what a patient needs.

big_questions.q: Nobody has ever caught HIV from a hug. Why are some people still afraid to sit beside a person with HIV?
big_questions.hint: Where do fears about illness come from, if they do not come from evidence? What would change a frightened person's mind?

big_questions.q: Your blood still holds the answer to a germ you met as a baby. Is your past gone, or is it still part of your body?
big_questions.hint: Think of a scar, a tree's rings, or the layers in a rock. What else keeps a record without a brain?

story.title: Six Yellow Wells
story.note: For parents. Real: Sellappan Nirmala, a 32-year-old microbiology student in Madras (now Chennai). Her teacher, Dr Suniti Solomon. Her husband, Veerappan Ramamoorthy, and his scooter. More than 80 blood samples collected over about three months, with no gloves. The serum kept in the fridge at home. The test done at the Christian Medical College in Vellore, 200 kilometres away, in 1986. Six samples turning yellow. The promise of secrecy. The second test in the United States. The health minister's announcement in the Tamil Nadu Assembly in May 1986, with both women in the visitors' gallery, and the disbelief that followed. Imagined: every conversation, Nirmala's thoughts, how the couple travelled to Vellore, the box of ice and the details of the laboratory. The women who gave blood had been arrested for sex work, which means being paid for sex. They were held in a government home called the Vigilance Home. The story says only that the police had arrested them. Tell your child as much as suits them.
text: Nirmala did not want this project. She was thirty-two, a student of microbiology at the medical college in Madras, and she needed a subject for her research. She had studied a disease that people catch from rats and dogs. That was work she understood.
"Look for AIDS," said her teacher, Dr Suniti Solomon.
"There is no AIDS in India, madam. Everybody says so. They tested hundreds of blood samples from Bombay and found nothing."
"Everybody says so," Dr Solomon agreed. "Nobody has looked here. That is a different thing."

So, at the end of 1985, Nirmala began to look. The illness was new to the world. Doctors knew that a virus caused it and that the virus passed from person to person in blood. They knew that people could carry the virus for years and feel perfectly well.
That was the part that troubled her. She said so one evening, while Dr Solomon was setting up a small laboratory with machines borrowed from her husband, who was a heart surgeon.
"Madam, if I take blood from a woman who feels well and looks well, what can the blood possibly show? You cannot see a virus. And if she had a fever from the virus, it would have gone long ago."
Dr Solomon was wiping a glass tube. "You are right. We will not see the virus, and we will not look for the virus. We will look for what her body has done about the virus."
"Antibodies."

"Antibodies. If the virus has ever been in her blood, her body has answered. It goes on answering every day, whether she feels anything or not. Her face can tell you nothing. Her blood keeps a record."

Every morning before her classes, Nirmala's husband, Ramamoorthy, drove her on his scooter to a government home. The police sent women there after arresting them. The women had not been asked whether they wanted to live there. Nirmala sat with them and talked. Some laughed at her needle. Some held out an arm without a word. She had no gloves. Nobody had told her she might need them.
She did not tell the women what she was testing for. In those days almost nobody asked a patient's permission for a test. Today the law says they must be asked, and that is right.

In three months she had more than eighty small tubes of blood. In the little laboratory she spun each tube until the red cells sank and the clear, straw-coloured serum stood on top. She drew off the serum. There was no proper cold store, so she took the tubes home and put them in her own fridge, beside the milk and the curry leaves.

Madras had no machine for the test. The nearest was in Vellore, two hundred kilometres away, at the Christian Medical College. So one night in 1986 Nirmala and Ramamoorthy packed the tubes in a box of ice and took the train.

In the Vellore laboratory there was a flat plastic plate with rows of small wells, each no bigger than a drop of rain. A little of the virus's own protein was stuck to the bottom of every well. Into each well went serum from one woman.

"If her serum has antibodies that fit, they will stick to the protein," the doctor running the test told her. "Then we wash the plate. Everything that has not stuck goes down the sink. Last, we add a chemical that turns yellow wherever an antibody is still holding on."
"And if there are no antibodies?"
"Then the well stays clear as water."
They filled the wells and they waited. Nirmala watched the plate. She thought of the scooter rides in the early light. She thought of eighty arms held out to her.

The doctor added the last chemical. For a while nothing happened. Then, in one well, the faintest colour came, like a drop of weak tea. Then in another. The colour deepened. She counted, and counted again.
Six wells were yellow.

Nobody spoke. Nirmala knew six numbers, and each number was a woman. She had seen all six of them laugh and scold and comb their hair. None of them had looked ill. Their bodies had known for months what no person in India knew, and had written it down where only this plate could read it.
"You will tell no one," the doctor said. "Not until we are certain."

Blood was then tested again in the United States, in another way. The answer was the same. In May, the health minister of Tamil Nadu stood up in the Assembly and announced that the virus had reached India. Nirmala and Dr Solomon sat in the visitors' gallery and listened.
Many people refused to believe it. Some said the test was wrong. Some said the two women had made a mistake.

They had not. Because the country now knew, the country could act. Blood for transfusion began to be tested. Clinics opened. Dr Solomon spent the rest of her life caring for people with HIV in Chennai, at a time when many hospitals turned them away.
Nirmala finished her research and handed it in the next year. She went to work at the King Institute in Chennai, and she retired quietly in 2010. For thirty years almost nobody knew her name.

In 2016 a reporter came to her home and wrote her story down at last. Nirmala had looked into the women's faces every morning for three months and learned nothing. Then she had looked at a plate of plastic wells for an hour, and their blood had told her.
story.epiphany: The women looked and felt well, so nobody could tell who carried the virus. The test did not look for the virus at all. It looked for antibodies, which a body goes on making for as long as the virus is there. Six wells turned yellow because six women's blood held antibodies that fit the virus's protein. A person's face showed nothing, and their blood held a record that a test could read.
ask: Why could nobody tell which women carried the virus just by looking at them?
The test did not look for the virus. What did it look for, and why does that work?
If one of the women had caught the virus only a week before, what might her well have shown? Why?
The women were not asked before they were tested. Why does the law now say that people must be asked?
Many people would not believe the result. What would you want to see before you believed it?
