experiments.title: The Titre Test: how much can you weaken a sample before the test misses it?
experiments.context: In this experiment three tumblers of water stand for the blood of three patients. A little washing powder stands for antibodies, and turmeric water is the test. You make each sample weaker in steps and test every step. You will find out which patient has the most, and at which step the test stops seeing it.
experiments.question: A sample turns turmeric red. If you make the sample 4 times weaker again and again, at which step does the red stop? Is the step the same for all three patients?
experiments.predict: Guess first. The three samples look alike. Will they all stop turning red at the same step? At which step do you think the red will stop: 4 times weaker, 16, 64 or 256? Write your guess, and write the reason for it.
experiments.fair_test: Change only one thing: how weak the sample is. Use the same spoon to measure every time, and rinse it in clean water after every katori, so that no strong liquid is carried into a weak one. Add the same amount of turmeric water to every katori. Stir the turmeric water before each spoonful, because the powder sinks. Judge every colour beside the plain-water katori, in the same light, one minute after adding the turmeric.
results_table: Titre (the weakest step still red or orange)

materials.item: washing powder for clothes, or a few shavings from a bar of washing soap
turmeric powder
glass or steel tumblers
small katoris, small tumblers or cups. A white ice tray with big wells also works
a tablespoon and a teaspoon
tap water, and a mug of clean water for rinsing the spoon
paper slips or tape for labels, a pencil and a notebook
a sheet of white paper to stand the katoris on

experiments.safety: Washing powder stings the eyes, so wash hands after the test and do not rub your eyes. Nobody tastes anything. Turmeric stains cloth and stone, so work on a steel plate or old newspaper.

schedule.what: A grown-up makes three mystery samples. The child weakens each one in steps, tests every step with turmeric water, finds each titre and writes what it shows.

experiments.record: Fill in the table with the colour of every katori: red, orange or yellow. Circle the weakest step that is still red or orange for each patient. That number is the titre. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: the titre of each patient's sample
example_chart.y: Titre (how many times weaker the sample still turned turmeric red)
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers depend on your washing powder and your water.

setup.art: Three steel tumblers of clear water labelled 1, 2 and 3 on a kitchen counter, beside a fourth tumbler of cloudy yellow turmeric water with a teaspoon in it.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up makes three mystery samples. You make a tumbler of turmeric water for testing.

setup.art: A row of five small katoris on white paper, with a child's hand moving one tablespoon of liquid from the first katori to the second, and a mug of rinse water beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Make a row of five. Each katori is 4 times weaker than the one before.

setup.art: The same row of five katoris after the turmeric water was added: the first three are red, the fourth is orange and the fifth is yellow, with a sixth yellow katori standing apart for comparison.
setup.caption: 3. Add one teaspoon of turmeric water to each. Compare each colour with the plain-water katori.

setup.art: A child writing the colours into a table in a notebook and drawing a circle round the last red step.
setup.caption: 4. Write down every colour. The weakest step that is still red or orange is the titre.

flow.do: 1. Do this part where your child cannot see. 2. Stir one pinch of washing powder into a tumbler of water. 3. Put 1 tablespoon of that liquid into a second tumbler and fill it with plain water. 4. Fill a third tumbler with plain water only. 5. Label them 1, 2 and 3 in any order, and write the order down secretly.
flow.say: These three tumblers are blood samples from three patients. One patient has a lot of antibody against a germ. One has a little. One has none. They look the same. Your test will tell them apart.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to make three mystery samples. They are pretend blood from three patients. You must not see which is which.
flow.parent: Check your powder once before you start. Put a spoon of the first tumbler's liquid in a katori and add a little turmeric water. It must turn clearly red. If it turns only orange, add another pinch of powder to the tumbler.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Titre Test. Here a grown-up secretly makes three samples that stand for the blood of three patients.

flow.do: 1. Stir half a teaspoon of turmeric into half a tumbler of water. 2. Put 4 tablespoons of plain water in one katori and add 1 teaspoon of turmeric water. 3. Stand this katori to one side. 4. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: This yellow katori has no washing powder. It shows what 'no' looks like. Now guess. At which step will the red stop? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Make the turmeric water. Make one katori with plain water and turmeric. That yellow is your 'no' colour. Now write your guess and your reason.
flow.parent: Accept any guess that comes with a reason. Do not say whether it is right. Turmeric does not dissolve in water, so the test liquid is cloudy. That is fine.
flow.context: This step of the Titre Test makes the yellow test liquid and a plain katori to compare against. Then you guess.

flow.do: 1. Stand five katoris in a row on white paper. 2. Put 4 tablespoons of Patient 1's sample in the first. 3. Put 3 tablespoons of plain water in each of the other four. 4. Move 1 tablespoon from the first katori to the second and stir. 5. Rinse the spoon. 6. Move 1 tablespoon from the second to the third, and so on to the fifth.
flow.say: One spoon of sample and three spoons of water make four spoons. So the second katori is 4 times weaker than the first. How many times weaker is the third?
flow.kid: Make a row of five katoris. Move one spoon along each time. Stir and rinse the spoon every time. Each katori is 4 times weaker.

ask.q: The second katori is 4 times weaker. How many times weaker is the third, and the fourth?

flow.parent: Rinsing the spoon matters. A wet spoon from a strong katori carries enough powder to change a weak one.
flow.context: This step of the Titre Test makes Patient 1's sample weaker in four steps. Each step is 4 times weaker than the one before.

flow.do: 1. Stir the turmeric water. 2. Add 1 teaspoon of it to each of the five katoris and stir each. 3. Wait one minute. 4. Hold each katori beside the plain yellow one. 5. Write red, orange or yellow for each in the table.
flow.say: Look at each katori beside the plain yellow one. Is it redder? Which is the weakest step that still shows any red or orange?
flow.kid: Add one teaspoon of turmeric water to each katori. Wait one minute. Compare each with the plain yellow katori. Write the colour of each one.
flow.parent: The change from red to yellow often passes through orange over one or two steps. Count orange as a weak yes. If all five are red, the sample was too strong. Make it again with half a pinch.
flow.context: This step of the Titre Test adds turmeric water to Patient 1's five katoris and reads the colours.

flow.do: 1. Empty and rinse the five katoris. 2. Repeat the whole row for Patient 2. 3. Write the colours. 4. Rinse again and repeat for Patient 3. 5. Circle each patient's titre in the table.
flow.say: Now do the same for the other two patients. Keep everything the same. Only the sample changes.
flow.kid: Rinse the katoris. Do the same for Patient 2. Then for Patient 3. Circle the weakest red step for each patient.
flow.parent: Keep the plain yellow katori through all three rows as the comparison. One patient's row should stay yellow all the way along.
flow.context: This step of the Titre Test repeats the row of five for Patient 2 and Patient 3, so that the three can be compared.

flow.do: 1. Point to the weakest katori of the strongest patient, which stayed yellow. 2. Ask whether it has any washing powder in it. 3. Wait for an answer and a reason.
flow.say: This katori stayed yellow. The test says no. Think about how we made it. Is there any washing powder in it at all?
flow.kid: Look at the last yellow katori of the strongest patient. The test says no. Is there really no washing powder in it? Think how you made it.

check.q: A katori was made by weakening a red sample 256 times. It stays yellow. What does that show?
options: It holds some, but too little for the test
The turmeric has stopped working
It holds no washing powder at all
check.why: You made that katori from the red sample, so some washing powder must be in it. There is too little to change the turmeric. A real blood test has the same limit in the first weeks of an infection. Picking 'none at all' means trusting the test more than what you know you put in.

flow.parent: This is the main point of the test. A 'no' from a test means 'not enough to find', which is different from 'none'.
flow.context: This step of the Titre Test asks what a yellow result really means, using a katori that you know holds a little washing powder.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to say which patient had the most and how they know. 2. Show your secret note of which tumbler was which. 3. Only now explain what the model stands for. 4. Your child writes the three sentences.
flow.say: Which patient had the most, and what is your evidence? Now I will show you what I made. In a real laboratory, the washing powder would be antibodies and the turmeric would be the test chemicals.
flow.kid: Say which patient had the most. Say how you know. Check with the grown-up's secret note. Then write what you thought, what you saw and why.

ask.q: Patient 3's row stayed yellow all along. Does that prove Patient 3 never met the germ?
good: No. They may have met it only days ago, in the window period
It shows there is not enough antibody to find
You would test again in a few weeks

flow.parent: The titre of the first tumbler should be about two steps higher than the titre of the weak one, because you made the weak one about 16 times weaker. Tell your child this is a model. Washing powder is not an antibody. What is real is the method: laboratories do weaken blood serum step by step and report the titre.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Titre Test. Here you say what you found, check it against the grown-up's secret note and write it down.

experiments.title: The Red Line Test: what does your skin do after one firm stroke?
experiments.context: In this experiment you draw one light line and one firm line on the inside of your forearm with something blunt. Nothing breaks the skin. Then you watch the two lines for ten minutes with a clock. You will find out whether your skin answers a harmless stroke, how fast, and for how long.
experiments.question: After a light stroke and a firm stroke with a blunt tool, does the skin change colour or rise? How many seconds does the change take to appear, and how many minutes to fade?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the light stroke and the firm stroke leave the same mark? How long will a mark take to appear, and how long to go? Write your guesses, and write the reason for each.
experiments.fair_test: Change only one thing: how firmly you press. Use the same blunt tool, the same arm and lines of the same length, about 5 centimetres. Draw the two lines three finger-widths apart so that they do not join. Look at the same times after each stroke. Then repeat on a second person, because skins differ.
results_table: Firm stroke: width of the mark (mm)

materials.item: something blunt and smooth: the rounded end of a steel spoon handle, or a pen with its cap on
a clock or phone timer that shows seconds
a ruler marked in millimetres
a ball pen to mark the ends of each line
a torch or a sunny window
a notebook and pencil

experiments.safety: Use only a blunt, smooth tool. Never use a fingernail, a pin, a compass point or anything sharp, and never press hard enough to hurt. Do not test on skin that has a rash, a cut, sunburn or eczema. In a few people the firm line rises into an itchy ridge. This is harmless and goes in about half an hour. Do not scratch it.

schedule.what: Draw a light line and a firm line on the forearm with a blunt tool. Watch both for ten minutes and record the changes. Repeat on a second person.

experiments.record: Fill in the table at each time. Draw a line graph for the firm stroke, with the time along the bottom and the width of the mark up the side. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: width of the mark after one firm stroke
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished graph can look like. Your skin will give different numbers, and some people's skin shows very little.

setup.art: A child's left forearm resting palm up on a table, with two small pen dots marking where a line will be drawn, and a steel spoon held by its bowl with the rounded handle end pointing at the skin.
setup.caption: 1. Rest your forearm palm up. Hold a spoon so that the rounded end of the handle touches the skin.

setup.art: The same forearm with the spoon handle being drawn firmly along the skin for about five centimetres, and a phone timer running beside the arm.
setup.caption: 2. Draw one light line. Three finger-widths away, draw one firm line. Start the timer.

setup.art: The same forearm a minute later, lit from the side by a torch, with a faint line where the light stroke was and a wider darker band where the firm stroke was, and a ruler laid across the band.
setup.caption: 3. Shine a light from the side. Measure how wide the firm mark is at each time.

flow.do: 1. Your child rests one forearm on the table, palm up. 2. Show the blunt tool and say what you will do. 3. Ask for the guesses and the reasons. 4. Your child writes them down.
flow.say: I will draw one light line and one firm line on your arm with this spoon handle. It will not hurt. What will your skin do? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Rest your arm palm up. You will draw two lines with a blunt spoon handle. Guess what your skin will do. Write your reason.
flow.parent: Check the skin first. If your child has eczema or a rash on the forearm, be the test person yourself and let your child do the stroking and timing.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Red Line Test. Here you choose the tool and guess what a stroke on the skin will do.

flow.do: 1. Mark two dots 5 centimetres apart. 2. Draw the tool lightly from dot to dot, as lightly as a feather. 3. Start the timer. 4. Look at 15 seconds, 30 seconds, 1 minute and 2 minutes. 5. Write the colour each time, and whether the line is raised.
flow.say: That was the light stroke. Watch the line. Tell me what you see at each time. Run a fingertip over it. Is it raised?
flow.kid: Draw one very light line. Start the timer. Look at 15 seconds, 30 seconds, 1 minute and 2 minutes. Write what you see.
flow.parent: A light stroke often leaves a pale line for a minute or two, or nothing at all. On brown skin a mark may look darker or lighter and not red. Light from the side helps.
flow.context: This step of the Red Line Test is the light stroke. You watch the line for two minutes.

flow.do: 1. Three finger-widths from the first line, draw a firm line of the same length. 2. Press about as hard as you press to rub out pencil. 3. Start the timer. 4. Look at 15 and 30 seconds, then at 1, 2, 3, 5 and 10 minutes. 5. Each time, measure the width of the mark and feel whether it is raised.
flow.say: That was the firm stroke. It should not hurt. Now watch. When does the colour come? How wide does it get? When does it start to fade?
flow.kid: Draw one firm line. It must not hurt. Start the timer. Measure the mark at each time. Feel if it is raised. Write it all down.
flow.parent: In most people a line of colour shows within half a minute, spreads a little wider than the stroke, and fades in five to fifteen minutes. In some people the line also rises a little after one to three minutes. If nothing shows, try once more a little more firmly on the upper arm. If still nothing shows, that is a real result. Write it down.
flow.context: This step of the Red Line Test is the firm stroke. You measure the mark for ten minutes.

flow.do: 1. While the first arm fades, do the firm stroke on a second person. 2. Use the same tool and the same pressure. 3. Record at 30 seconds, 1 minute and 3 minutes. 4. Compare the two people.
flow.say: Now we test my arm in the same way. Do you think my skin will do the same as yours? Why?
flow.kid: Do the firm stroke on a second person. Use the same tool. Record at 30 seconds, 1 minute and 3 minutes. Compare.
flow.parent: People differ a great deal. About one person in twenty to fifty has skin that rises into a clear ridge. Doctors call this skin writing, or dermatographism. It is harmless.
flow.context: This step of the Red Line Test repeats the firm stroke on a second person, to see whether all skins answer in the same way.

flow.do: 1. Ask what your child saw, and what they think made the mark. 2. Listen to the whole answer. 3. Then give the scientists' explanation. 4. Your child writes the three sentences.
flow.say: Nothing went into your skin, and the spoon has gone. So what made the mark come later, and spread? Tell me your idea first.
flow.kid: The spoon touched you for one second. The mark came later. What do you think made it? Say your idea. Then write three sentences.

ask.q: The mark came after the spoon had gone, and it spread wider than the stroke. What does that tell you about who made it?
good: My skin made it, the spoon did not
Something spread out from where I pressed
It is the body answering, like a mosquito bump

check.q: After a firm stroke, a mark appears later and spreads wider than the stroke. What does this show?
options: The spoon left colour on the skin
The skin answered with chemicals that spread
The skin was badly damaged
check.why: The delay and the spreading show that the body is acting. The usual explanation is that pressure makes mast cells in the skin release a little histamine. The histamine widens the small blood vessels nearby. Picking 'the spoon left colour' misses that the mark came after the spoon had gone.

flow.parent: The explanation, to give only after your child's own idea: the skin holds mast cells packed with histamine. Firm pressure makes some of them release a little. Histamine widens small blood vessels, which gives the colour, and makes them leaky, which gives the swelling. The doctor Thomas Lewis studied this in London in the 1920s. An allergy uses the same cells and the same chemical. The difference is the trigger, which in an allergy is IgE meeting an allergen.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Red Line Test. Here you say what you saw and what you think caused it, and then hear the scientists' explanation.

activities.title: The Bite Survey: who makes the biggest mosquito bump?
activities.context: In this activity you ask the people at home what happens to their skin when a mosquito bites them. You compare the answers. You will find out whether the same bite gives the same bump on everyone, and start asking who makes the bump.

materials.item: three or more people of different ages, at home or on the phone
a notebook and pencil
a ruler marked in millimetres, if anyone has a bite today

activities.record: Make a table with one row for each person. Write their age, how big their bump usually gets, how long it itches, and whether it was different when they were small. Under the table, write one thing you noticed and one thing you wonder.

setup.art: A girl with a notebook asking her grandmother a question on a balcony in the evening, while the grandmother points to a small bump on her own wrist.
setup.caption: 1. Ask each person: how big is your mosquito bump, and how long does it itch?

setup.art: A notebook page with a table of four rows, showing names, ages, small drawings of bumps of different sizes and the number of hours of itching.
setup.caption: 2. Write the answers in a table and compare them.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to question three people, and answer for themselves too. 2. The questions are below. 3. If anyone has a bite today, measure it with the ruler.
flow.say: Ask each person two things. How big does your mosquito bump get? How long does it itch? Ask the oldest person if it was different when they were a child.
flow.kid: Ask three people about their mosquito bumps. How big? How long does it itch? Was it different when they were small? Write the answers.
flow.parent: Phone a grandparent if only two people are at home. People who have lived many years with mosquitoes often say that they hardly react any more.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bite Survey. Here you collect answers from three or more people.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask what is the same and what differs. 3. Ask the question below and wait for an answer and a reason.
flow.say: The mosquito does the same thing to everyone. So why are the bumps different? And the mosquito has flown away. Who makes the bump? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at your table. Are all the bumps the same? The mosquito has gone. So who makes the bump? Say what you think and why.

ask.q: The mosquito has flown away before the bump rises. Who makes the bump?
good: It is my body answering something the mosquito left

flow.parent: Do not explain yet. A good answer is that the body makes the bump. The differences between people are the clue.
flow.context: This step of the Bite Survey compares the answers and asks who makes the bump.

flow.do: 1. After your child has answered, read the explanation in the parent note aloud. 2. Ask your child to write one thing they noticed and one thing they wonder.
flow.say: A mosquito leaves a little saliva in your skin. Your body has met it before and answers it. The bump is your answer. A baby bitten for the very first time usually gets no bump.
flow.kid: The mosquito leaves saliva in your skin. Your body answers it. The bump is your body's answer. Write one thing you wonder.
flow.parent: The fuller picture: the body makes IgE antibodies against proteins in mosquito saliva. They sit on mast cells in the skin. At the next bite the mast cells release histamine, which gives the bump and the itch. After years of many bites, some people's bodies stop reacting. The rest of the unit explains each of these words.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Bite Survey. Here you hear what a mosquito bump is, and write down what you wonder.

activities.title: Peg Antibodies: why does an antibody have two arms?
activities.context: In this activity clothes pegs are antibodies and squares of card are germs. First you use single pegs, which have one arm. Then you tie pegs in pairs to make two arms. You will find out what two arms can do that one arm cannot.

materials.item: clothes pegs with springs
rubber bands or short pieces of thread
squares of thick card about as wide as your palm, cut from an old carton
a pair of scissors, a pencil and a notebook

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the thick card. Pegs can pinch fingers.
activities.record: Draw the clump you made, with the pegs as Y shapes. Write how many germs came up when you lifted one germ, first with single pegs and then with double pegs.

setup.art: Eight squares of brown card spread on a table, each with one wooden clothes peg clipped to its edge.
setup.caption: 1. Clip one single peg to each card germ. Lift one germ and count how many come up.

setup.art: Two clothes pegs tied back to back with a rubber band so that their jaws point in opposite directions, held in a child's hand.
setup.caption: 2. Tie two pegs back to back with a rubber band. This is an antibody with two arms.

setup.art: Several card squares joined into one chain by double pegs, each double peg holding two squares, with a child lifting the whole chain by one square.
setup.caption: 3. Clip each double peg to two germs. Lift one germ and count again.

flow.do: 1. Spread the 8 card germs on the table. 2. Clip one single peg to each. 3. Ask what will happen when one germ is lifted, and why. 4. Your child lifts one germ.
flow.say: Each peg is an antibody with one arm. Every germ has one. If you lift one germ, how many will come up? Why?
flow.kid: Clip one peg on each card germ. Guess how many come up when you lift one. Now lift one and count.
flow.parent: Only one germ comes up. The germs are covered but they are still free to spread.
flow.context: This is the first step of Peg Antibodies. Here every card germ gets an antibody that has only one arm.

flow.do: 1. Take the pegs off. 2. Tie the pegs in pairs, back to back, with rubber bands. 3. Ask for a new guess. 4. Your child clips each double peg to two different germs. 5. Your child lifts one germ and counts.
flow.say: Now each antibody has two arms. Clip each one to two germs. If you lift one germ now, how many will come up? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Tie the pegs in pairs. Clip each pair to two germs. Guess how many come up. Lift one germ and count.
flow.parent: Depending on how the pegs are placed, a few germs or all eight come up as one clump. Let your child find the way that joins all eight. Seven double pegs are enough to join eight germs in a chain.
flow.context: This step of Peg Antibodies ties pegs in pairs to make antibodies with two arms, and joins the card germs with them.

flow.do: 1. Your child plays a phagocyte and picks up germs with one hand. 2. Count the grabs needed for 8 loose germs, then for one clump. 3. Ask what two arms did that one arm could not. 4. Your child draws the clump.
flow.say: Be a phagocyte, a cell who swallows germs. How many grabs for eight loose germs? How many for the clump? So what are two arms good for?
flow.kid: Be a phagocyte. Count your grabs for loose germs. Count your grabs for a clump. Say what two arms are good for. Draw the clump.

check.q: What can an antibody with two arms do that an antibody with one arm cannot?
options: Fit two different kinds of germ
Kill a germ by squeezing
Join two germs together
check.why: Two arms let one antibody hold two germs, so many antibodies tie many germs into a clump. The two tips are the same, so they fit the same kind of germ. Picking 'kill' treats the antibody as a weapon, but it only holds.

flow.parent: Real clumping is called agglutination. Doctors use it to find a person's blood group.
flow.context: This is the last step of Peg Antibodies. Here you compare loose germs with a clump and say what two arms are for.

activities.title: Boylston's Count: was inoculation safer than catching smallpox?
activities.context: In 1721, smallpox struck the town of Boston in America. A doctor called Zabdiel Boylston inoculated some people, after hearing what an enslaved African man called Onesimus had said. Boylston counted who lived and who died. In this activity you use his real numbers to decide whether inoculation was safer.

materials.item: squared paper, or plain paper and a ruler
two colour pencils
a pencil and a notebook. A calculator is allowed

activities.record: Draw two grids of 100 squares. On one, shade the number who died out of every 100 people who caught smallpox the usual way. On the other, shade the number who died out of every 100 who were inoculated. Write one sentence that says what the grids show, and one question you would still ask.

setup.art: A notebook page showing four numbers in two rows: caught smallpox the usual way, 5,759 people and 844 died. Inoculated, 247 people and 6 died.
setup.caption: 1. Read the four numbers that were counted in Boston in 1721.

setup.art: Two grids of ten by ten squares side by side on squared paper, the first with fifteen squares shaded red and the second with two squares shaded blue.
setup.caption: 2. Work out how many died out of every 100 in each group, and shade the squares.

flow.do: 1. Read the numbers aloud. 2. About 5,759 people caught smallpox the usual way, and 844 of them died. 3. Boylston inoculated 247 people, and 6 of them died. 4. Ask the question below and wait.
flow.say: Six inoculated people died, and 844 other people died. Does that prove inoculation was safer? What else do you need to look at? Why?
flow.kid: Read the four numbers. Six is much smaller than 844. Is that enough to say inoculation was safer? Say why or why not.

ask.q: Why is it unfair to compare 6 deaths with 844 deaths?
good: Only 247 people were inoculated but thousands caught it the usual way
We need to know how many died out of the same number

flow.parent: The point to reach is that the groups are of very different sizes. The count of deaths must be compared with the size of each group.
flow.context: This is the first step of Boylston's Count. Here you read the real numbers from Boston in 1721 and ask how to compare them.

flow.do: 1. For each group, divide the number who died by the number in the group. 2. Multiply by 100. 3. Round to the nearest whole number. 4. Shade that many squares on a grid of 100.
flow.say: Let's find how many died out of every hundred. 844 divided by 5,759, times 100. Then 6 divided by 247, times 100. Guess each answer before you work it out.
flow.kid: Divide 844 by 5,759. Multiply by 100. Then divide 6 by 247. Multiply by 100. Shade that many squares on each grid.
flow.parent: 844 ÷ 5,759 × 100 is about 14.7, so shade 15 squares. 6 ÷ 247 × 100 is about 2.4, so shade 2 squares. To estimate without a calculator: 5,759 is nearly 5,800, and one hundredth of that is 58. 844 ÷ 58 is between 14 and 15.
flow.context: This step of Boylston's Count turns each pair of numbers into deaths out of every 100 people, and shades two grids.

flow.do: 1. Compare the two grids. 2. Ask what they show. 3. Ask whether the comparison is fully fair. 4. Tell the story of Onesimus from the parent note. 5. Your child writes a sentence and a question.
flow.say: What do the two grids show? Now be a careful scientist. Could anything other than inoculation explain the difference? What would you want to check?
flow.kid: Compare your two grids. Say what they show. Think of one thing that could make the comparison unfair. Write a sentence and a question.

ask.q: Could anything else explain why fewer inoculated people died?
good: Maybe healthier or richer people chose inoculation
Maybe they were better looked after
The inoculated group is small, so chance matters more
Inoculated people could pass smallpox to others, and those deaths were not counted

flow.parent: About 15 in 100 died after catching smallpox the usual way, and about 2 in 100 after inoculation. That is about six times safer. Boylston's count was one of the first times anyone used numbers to judge a medical treatment. The knowledge came from Onesimus, a West African man enslaved in the house of the minister Cotton Mather. He told Mather he had been inoculated as a boy. Most Boston doctors refused to try it, and one reason was that the knowledge came from Africans.
flow.context: This is the last step of Boylston's Count. Here you compare the two grids, ask whether the comparison is fair and hear where the knowledge came from.

activities.title: The Helper Count: a bean model of HIV, with and without medicine
activities.context: In this activity 20 beans in a katori stand for the helper T cells in a drop of blood. Each roll of a die is one year with HIV. You run the model with no medicine and then with medicine, and draw both as line graphs. You will see why a person with HIV can feel well for years, and what the medicine changes.

materials.item: rajma, chana or any large dried beans
two katoris, one for the blood and one for spare beans
a die
squared paper, a ruler and two colour pencils

activities.record: Make a table with a row for each year and columns for the number of beans in Run 1 and Run 2. Draw both runs on one line graph, with years along the bottom and beans up the side. Draw a dotted line across at 4 beans. Write two sentences on how the lines differ.

setup.art: A steel katori holding twenty red rajma beans, a second katori of spare beans, and a die on a table beside a sheet of squared paper.
setup.caption: 1. Put 20 beans in a katori. They are the helper T cells in a drop of blood.

setup.art: A child's hand taking four beans out of the first katori after rolling a four on the die, and then dropping two beans back in.
setup.caption: 2. Each year, roll the die and take out that many beans. Then put 2 back.

setup.art: A line graph on squared paper with one red line falling from 20 to below a dotted line at 4, and one blue line that falls for three years and then climbs back up.
setup.caption: 3. Draw one line with no medicine and one line with medicine.

flow.do: 1. Put 20 beans in the katori. 2. Explain the rules. 3. Each year the die shows how many helper T cells HIV destroys. 4. Then the body makes 2 new ones. 5. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Each bean is 50 helper T cells in a pinhead drop of blood. Each year HIV destroys some, and the body adds two beans. What will the line look like over ten years? Why?
flow.kid: Put 20 beans in the katori. Each year you roll the die and take out that many. Then you put 2 back. Guess what the graph will look like.
flow.parent: Twenty beans stand for 1,000 helper T cells in a cubic millimetre of blood, which is a healthy number. Four beans stand for 200, the level below which doctors speak of AIDS.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Helper Count. Here you set up 20 beans as helper T cells and learn the rules of the model.

flow.do: 1. Run 1 has no medicine. 2. Roll the die, take out that many beans, then put 2 back. 3. Write the number left. 4. Repeat for each year until 4 or fewer beans are left, or 15 years have passed.
flow.say: This is Run 1, with no medicine. Roll, take out, put two back, and write the number. Tell me when you reach four beans or fewer.
flow.kid: Run 1 has no medicine. Roll the die. Take out that many beans. Put 2 back. Write the number left. Stop at 4 beans or fewer.
flow.parent: The count usually reaches 4 after about 8 to 13 rolls. It goes up in years when the die shows 1, and that is fine. Real counts wobble too.
flow.context: This step of the Helper Count runs the model with no medicine, one roll of the die for each year.

flow.do: 1. Start Run 2 again with 20 beans. 2. Play years 1, 2 and 3 as before. 3. From year 4 the person takes medicine. 4. Now HIV destroys no beans, and the body still adds 2 each year, up to 20. 5. Write the number each year for 12 years.
flow.say: Run 2 starts the same way. After year 3 the person starts medicine. The medicine stops the virus from copying. What will the line do now? Why?
flow.kid: Start again with 20 beans. Play 3 years as before. Then start the medicine. Now take out no beans. Add 2 each year, up to 20.
flow.parent: The count climbs back towards 20. In real life the recovery is slower when treatment starts late, which is why doctors now start medicine as soon as HIV is found.
flow.context: This step of the Helper Count runs the model again. This time the person starts medicine after three years.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws both runs on one graph. 2. Draw a dotted line across at 4 beans. 3. Ask the questions below. 4. Your child writes two sentences.
flow.say: Look at Run 1. For how many years was the count above the dotted line? Would the person have felt ill in those years? What did the medicine change?
flow.kid: Draw both runs on one graph. Draw a dotted line at 4 beans. Say what the medicine changed. Write two sentences.

check.q: In the model, the medicine made the helper T cell count rise again. What did the medicine do?
options: It stopped the virus destroying cells
It made new helper T cells
It removed every virus from the body
check.why: The medicine stops HIV from copying, so no more helper T cells are destroyed. The body itself makes the new cells. The medicine does not remove the virus, which stays hidden in resting cells. That is why it is taken every day for life.

flow.parent: Say plainly that this is a model with made-up numbers. Real bodies make and lose many millions of helper T cells every day, and people differ. What the model gets right is the long quiet fall, and that the medicine stops the loss while the body does the repair.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Helper Count. Here you draw both runs as line graphs and say what the medicine changed.

activities.title: The Label Hunt: find the allergens in your kitchen
activities.context: In this activity you read the labels of packed foods in your kitchen. Food makers in India must print which common allergens a food contains. You will find out which allergens turn up most often, and which turn up where you would not expect them.

materials.item: packed foods from the kitchen shelf, such as biscuits, namkeen, noodles, chocolate, sauce, bread and breakfast cereal
a notebook and pencil
a magnifying glass, if the print is very small

activities.record: Make a table with one row for each packet. Write the food, what the label says after 'Contains', and what it says after 'May contain'. Count how many packets name each allergen and draw a bar chart. Circle one result that surprised you.

setup.art: A row of eight food packets on a kitchen shelf, including a biscuit packet, a noodle packet, a chocolate bar and a bottle of sauce, with a child reaching for one.
setup.caption: 1. Collect eight packed foods from the kitchen.

setup.art: The back of a biscuit packet seen close up, with a child's finger pointing at a line in bold print that begins with the word Contains.
setup.caption: 2. Find the line that begins 'Contains' near the list of ingredients. Write down what it says.

flow.do: 1. Collect 8 packets. 2. Before reading, ask your child to guess which allergen will appear on the most packets. 3. Ask for a reason.
flow.say: An allergen is a harmless thing that some bodies answer with an allergy. Wheat, milk, nuts, soya and egg are common ones. Which will be on the most packets? Why?
flow.kid: Collect 8 packets from the kitchen. Guess which allergen is on the most packets. Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Label Hunt. Here you collect eight packed foods and guess which allergen is the most common.

flow.do: 1. On each packet, find the list of ingredients. 2. Look for a line that begins 'Contains' or 'Allergen information'. 3. Write what it says. 4. Look for 'May contain' as well.
flow.say: Find the word 'Contains' on each packet. Read me what follows it. Is there a 'May contain' line too? What do you think that one means?
flow.kid: Find the word 'Contains' on each packet. Write what it says. Look for 'May contain' too.
flow.parent: 'Contains' lists allergens that are in the food. 'May contain' means that the same factory also handles that allergen, so a trace could get in. For a person with a severe allergy, a trace can be enough.
flow.context: This step of the Label Hunt reads the allergen lines on each packet and writes them in a table.

flow.do: 1. Count how many packets name each allergen. 2. Your child draws a bar chart. 3. Ask which result was a surprise. 4. Ask who needs these labels.
flow.say: Which allergen won? Did any food hold an allergen you did not expect? Who reads these lines every time they shop, and why?
flow.kid: Count the packets for each allergen. Draw a bar chart. Circle one surprise. Say who needs these labels.
flow.parent: Wheat and milk usually come first. Surprises are common: soya in chocolate, wheat in soy sauce, milk in some crisps, nuts in a biscuit that looks plain. A child with a food allergy and their family read every label, every time.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Label Hunt. Here you count the allergens, draw a bar chart and look for surprises.

activities.title: Two Meetings: draw what happens in an allergy
activities.context: In this activity you draw an allergy as a comic strip of four boxes. You draw the parts that nobody can see: the IgE antibodies, the mast cell and the histamine. Drawing it shows why an allergy never happens the first time a person meets an allergen.

materials.item: a sheet of plain paper folded into four boxes
a pencil and colour pencils

activities.record: Keep the finished comic strip in your notebook. Under it, write one sentence that answers this: why does nothing happen at the first meeting?

setup.art: A sheet of paper folded into four boxes, numbered one to four, with a pencil and colour pencils beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Fold a sheet into four boxes and number them.

setup.art: A child's finished four-box comic: a peanut protein meeting a B cell, Y shapes landing on a spotted mast cell, a second peanut protein linking two Y shapes, and dots bursting out of the cell beside a swollen blood vessel.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the first meeting, the waiting, the second meeting and the alarm.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what they think happens inside the skin in an allergy. 2. Let them sketch their own idea on scrap paper first. 3. Do not correct it yet.
flow.say: A child eats a prawn for the first time and is fine. The second time, her lips swell. What do you think happened inside her between the two meals? Sketch your idea.
flow.kid: A girl eats prawn once and is fine. The second time her lips swell. Sketch what you think changed inside her.
flow.parent: Any idea with a reason is welcome. Many children guess that the body 'got ready' in between, which is right.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Meetings. Here you sketch your own idea of what changes in the body between two meals.

flow.do: 1. Read the four captions aloud, one at a time. 2. Your child draws each box. 3. Box 1: a prawn protein meets a B cell. 4. Box 2: the B cell's IgE antibodies sit on a mast cell, stems down. 5. Box 3: a new prawn protein links two IgE antibodies. 6. Box 4: the mast cell releases histamine and a blood vessel swells.
flow.say: Draw the antibodies as small Y shapes. Draw the mast cell as a round cell full of dots. The dots are bags of histamine.
flow.kid: Draw four boxes. One: prawn protein meets a B cell. Two: Y shapes sit on a mast cell. Three: prawn protein links two Y shapes. Four: dots burst out.
flow.parent: The key detail is in box 3: one allergen must link two IgE antibodies on the same mast cell. A single antibody touched alone does not set the cell off.
flow.context: This step of Two Meetings draws the four stages of an allergy as a comic strip, including the parts nobody can see.

flow.do: 1. Your child compares the comic with their first sketch. 2. Ask the question below. 3. Your child writes one sentence under the comic.
flow.say: Look at your first sketch and your comic. What did you have right? Now tell me why nothing happens at the first meeting.
flow.kid: Compare your sketch and your comic. Say why nothing happens at the first meeting. Write it in one sentence.

check.q: Why does an allergic reaction not happen the first time a person meets an allergen?
options: The allergen is weaker the first time
No IgE against it sits on mast cells yet
Mast cells are made only after the first meeting
check.why: At the first meeting the body has no IgE that fits the allergen. It makes IgE afterwards, and the IgE settles on mast cells. Only then can the allergen set the mast cells off. The allergen itself is the same both times.

flow.context: This is the last step of Two Meetings. Here you compare your first idea with your comic and explain the first meeting.

games.title: Right Target, Wrong Target or Too Weak?
games.context: This is a card game about four things an immune system can do. It can work well, it can answer something harmless, it can attack the body, or it can be too weak. Each card describes something that happens to a person. You decide which of the four it is and say why.

printables.title: 24 case cards to cut out, with the answer on the back

items.f: Kavya had chickenpox when she was four. Now her cousin has it. She plays with him and stays well.
items.b: WORKING WELL. Her memory cells and antibodies from the first time stop the virus quickly.

items.f: A cut on Yazhini's knee turns red and warm. A week later it has healed.
items.b: WORKING WELL. Redness and warmth are signs of white blood cells arriving to deal with germs in the cut.

items.f: A baby gets a measles vaccine and has a slight fever a week later. After that the baby is protected.
items.b: WORKING WELL. The body answered the vaccine and made plasma cells and memory cells.

items.f: Meenakshi has a fever. A blood test finds IgM antibodies against dengue virus.
items.b: WORKING WELL. IgM is the first antibody made in a new infection. Her body is answering the virus.

items.f: A phagocyte swallows a clump of bacteria that are coated in antibodies.
items.b: WORKING WELL. The antibodies clumped and flagged the bacteria, and the phagocyte destroyed them.

items.f: A two-week-old baby meets a cold virus. Antibodies from the mother, already in the baby's blood, stick to the virus.
items.b: WORKING WELL. IgG crossed the placenta before birth. The baby borrows the mother's record for some months.

items.f: Farhan's lips swell and itch a few minutes after he eats prawn curry.
items.b: WRONG TARGET: ALLERGY. Prawn protein is harmless, but he has IgE against it. His mast cells released histamine.

items.f: Every year when the grass flowers, Lakshmi sneezes and her eyes water.
items.b: WRONG TARGET: ALLERGY. Her body answers harmless pollen. This is called hay fever.

items.f: A mosquito bites Divya. Ten minutes later there is an itchy bump.
items.b: WRONG TARGET: ALLERGY. The bump is a small allergic reaction to mosquito saliva. It is harmless.

items.f: Anu's chest feels tight and she wheezes when an old cotton mattress is beaten.
items.b: WRONG TARGET: ALLERGY. She is allergic to house dust mites. Histamine tightens the airways.

items.f: A woman gets an itchy rash all over, minutes after a penicillin injection.
items.b: WRONG TARGET: ALLERGY. Penicillin is harmless to most people. Her body has made IgE against penicillin. She must never be given penicillin again.

items.f: A bee stings a woman's hand. Within minutes her throat swells and she finds it hard to breathe.
items.b: WRONG TARGET: ALLERGY. This is anaphylaxis, a severe reaction all over the body. She needs adrenaline and an ambulance at once.

items.f: T cells destroy the cells in Nila's pancreas who make insulin. She now takes insulin every day.
items.b: WRONG TARGET: THE BODY. This is type 1 diabetes, an autoimmune disease.

items.f: Antibodies and T cells slowly damage a woman's thyroid gland. She feels tired and cold.
items.b: WRONG TARGET: THE BODY. This is Hashimoto's disease, an autoimmune disease. She takes thyroid hormone as a tablet.

items.f: When Rhea eats roti or bread, her immune system damages the lining of her own gut.
items.b: WRONG TARGET: THE BODY. This is coeliac disease. Gluten from wheat sets off an attack on her own gut. She stays well on rice, ragi and millets.

items.f: The joints of a grandmother's fingers are swollen and painful every morning. Her immune system is attacking them.
items.b: WRONG TARGET: THE BODY. This is rheumatoid arthritis, an autoimmune disease.

items.f: White patches slowly appear on Shreya's hands and face. The cells who make skin colour there have gone.
items.b: WRONG TARGET: THE BODY. This is vitiligo. Most scientists think the immune system destroys the colour-making cells. It is not catching.

items.f: After a sore throat caused by a bacterium, a child's antibodies against the bacterium also stick to her heart.
items.b: WRONG TARGET: THE BODY. This is rheumatic fever. A part of the bacterium looks like a part of the heart.

items.f: HIV has destroyed most of a man's helper T cells. A fungus that lives quietly in most mouths spreads down his throat.
items.b: TOO WEAK. This is AIDS. Without helper T cells, the defence is not switched on.

items.f: A baby is born with no working thymus and catches one infection after another.
items.b: TOO WEAK. T cells are tested and finished in the thymus. Without it the baby has very few.

items.f: A woman has been given a new kidney. She takes medicines that hold her immune system down, and she catches colds easily.
items.b: TOO WEAK, on purpose. The medicines stop her body attacking the new kidney. The cost is a weaker defence.

items.f: A person with HIV stops taking the medicine. Over the next years, the helper T cell count falls.
items.b: TOO WEAK. The medicine does not remove HIV. When it stops, the virus copies again and destroys helper T cells.

items.f: A girl is having strong medicines for cancer. They also harm the bone marrow, where white blood cells are made.
items.b: TOO WEAK, for a time. With fewer white blood cells she catches infections easily until the marrow recovers.

items.f: A woman of ninety gets a flu vaccine. It protects her less well than it protects her granddaughter.
items.b: TOO WEAK. The thymus shrinks with age, so an old body makes few new T cells and answers a vaccine less strongly.

printables.title: Four mats to copy onto four sheets of paper
items: WORKING WELL: the defence answers a real germ, and the person gets better or stays well.
WRONG TARGET, ALLERGY: the defence answers something harmless from outside.
WRONG TARGET, THE BODY: the defence attacks the person's own cells.
TOO WEAK: the defence does not answer strongly enough.

rules: Cut out the 24 cards. Shuffle them and put them in a pile with the case side up. Lay the four mats in a row.
On your turn, read the top card aloud. Say which mat it belongs on, and give your reason.
Turn the card over and read the back. If you chose the right mat, put the card on that mat and score 1 point.
If you chose the wrong mat, read the back aloud and slide the card under the pile. It will come round again.
The game ends when the pile is empty. The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: count how many cards you get right the first time. Play again another day and try to beat your score.

setup.art: Four sheets of paper in a row on a floor mat, each with a heading written in large letters, and a pile of small cards beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the four mats. Put the shuffled cards in a pile, case side up.

setup.art: A girl holding up one card and reading it aloud to her father, with her other hand pointing at one of the four mats.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card, choose a mat and say why.

setup.art: The same card turned over to show the answer on the back, being placed on the matching mat.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over to check. Right cards go on the mat. Wrong ones go under the pile.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Copy the four headings onto four sheets of paper. 3. Shuffle the cards and put them case side up. 4. Read the four mats aloud together.
flow.say: An immune system can do four things. It can work well. It can answer something harmless. It can attack the body. Or it can be too weak. Each card is one of these.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Write the four headings on four sheets. Shuffle the cards. Put them case side up.
flow.context: This is the first step of Right Target, Wrong Target or Too Weak? Here you set up the cards and the four mats.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to read a card. 2. The player names a mat and gives a reason. 3. Turn the card over to check. 4. A right card goes on its mat. A wrong one goes under the pile.
flow.say: Read the card. Ask yourself two things. What is the defence answering? And is that thing a real danger?
flow.kid: Read a card aloud. Choose a mat and say why. Turn the card over. Were you right?
flow.parent: The two allergy and autoimmune mats are mixed up most often. The question that separates them is whether the target comes from outside the body or is part of the body.
flow.context: This step of Right Target, Wrong Target or Too Weak? is the game itself. You sort each case and check the back.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Look at the four mats together. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at the two wrong-target mats. In both, the defence is working hard. So is a stronger immune system always a better one? Why?
flow.kid: Count your points. Look at the two wrong-target mats. Is a stronger immune system always better? Say why.

check.q: A child sneezes whenever she meets cat hair. What is her immune system doing?
options: It is too weak to fight cat germs
It is answering something harmless
It is attacking her own nose
check.why: Proteins on cat hair are harmless, and her body answers them with IgE and histamine. That is an allergy. Her defence is not weak. It is aimed at the wrong thing.

flow.context: This is the last step of Right Target, Wrong Target or Too Weak? Here you count the points and ask whether stronger always means better.

games.context: This is a card and dice game about how the body stops T cells from attacking it. Young T cells are tested in the thymus, and the ones who fit the body's own parts are removed. Then the T cells who passed meet germs. You will see that the test protects the body, and what happens when a T cell slips through.

items: a protein on red blood cells
a protein of the thyroid gland
