a protein of the lining of the joints
a protein of the gut lining

printables.title: Score sheet
items: Round 1, the thymus: T cells removed ____. T cells who passed ____. T cells who slipped through ____.
Round 2, the body: germs beaten ____ × 1 point = ____.
T cells who slipped through and were calmed ____ × 0 points.
T cells who slipped through and attacked the body ____ × 2 points taken away = ____.

rules: You need the cards, the Self List and one die. Shuffle the 20 T cell cards and put them face down. Shuffle the 12 germ cards and put them face down in a second pile.
Round 1 is the thymus. Turn over the T cell cards one at a time. If the card fits nothing on the Self List, the T cell passes. Put the card face up in a 'passed' row.

If the card fits something on the Self List, roll the die. On 1 to 5 the thymus removes this T cell, so put the card in the bin pile. On a 6 the thymus misses, and the T cell slips through. Put the card sideways in the 'passed' row.
Round 2 is the body. Turn over 8 germ cards one at a time. If a T cell in your 'passed' row fits the germ, the germ is beaten and you score 1 point.

Now look at each T cell who slipped through. Roll the die for each. On 1 to 3, a regulatory T cell calms this one down and nothing happens. On 4 to 6, the T cell attacks the body. Take away 2 points and say which part of the body is attacked.
Playing alone, play three times and add up your score. With others, take turns and compare scores. The highest score wins.

setup.art: A sheet of paper headed Self List with eight short lines of writing, beside a face-down pile of cards, a second smaller pile and one die.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the Self List, the two piles of cards and the die.

setup.art: A child turning over a card and holding it next to the Self List to compare, with a row of passed cards on one side and a small bin pile on the other.
setup.caption: 2. Round 1: check each T cell against the Self List. T cells who fit the body are removed, unless you roll a 6.

setup.art: A germ card turned face up beside the row of passed T cell cards, with a child pointing at the one T cell card that matches it.
setup.caption: 3. Round 2: turn over 8 germs. Score a point for each germ that one of your T cells fits.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards and the Self List. 2. Shuffle each pile. 3. Read the Self List aloud. 4. Ask the question below before any card is turned.
flow.say: T cells get their receptors by chance. So some will fit your own body. What should the body do with those, before it lets them out? Why?
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Read the Self List. Some T cells will fit your own body. What should happen to them? Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Thymus School. Here you set up the cards and think about T cells who fit the body's own parts.

flow.do: 1. Play Round 1. 2. Turn over each T cell card and check the Self List. 3. For a T cell who fits the body, roll the die. 4. Fill in the first line of the score sheet.
flow.say: You are the thymus. Check every T cell against the Self List. If one fits the body, roll. Only a six lets that one slip through.
flow.kid: Turn over each T cell. Does the card fit the Self List? If yes, roll the die. A 6 means this T cell slips through.
flow.parent: Usually seven or eight of the eight body-fitting T cells are removed, and sometimes one or two slip through. In a real thymus most young T cells die there, and far more are tested than in this game.
flow.context: This step of Thymus School is Round 1. You play the thymus and test every young T cell against the body's own parts.

flow.do: 1. Play Round 2. 2. Turn over 8 germ cards and look for a matching T cell each time. 3. Then roll for each T cell who slipped through. 4. Fill in the score sheet.
flow.say: Now the T cells who passed are out in the body. Here come the germs. Then we find out what the ones who slipped through will do.
flow.kid: Turn over 8 germs. Find a T cell for each. Score 1 for each match. Then roll for each T cell who slipped through.
flow.parent: With all twelve germ-fitting T cells passed, every germ is beaten. Points are lost only through T cells who slipped through and were not calmed.
flow.context: This step of Thymus School is Round 2. The T cells who passed meet germs, and any T cell who slipped through may attack the body.

flow.do: 1. Add up the score. 2. Ask what kind of illness an attack on the body is. 3. Ask the question in the check.
flow.say: When a slipped T cell attacked the thyroid or the joints, what kind of illness was that? And what did the roll of one to three stand for?
flow.kid: Add up your score. What is it called when a T cell attacks the body? What calmed some of them down?

check.q: Why does the thymus remove T cells whose receptors fit the body's own proteins?
options: The body has too many T cells
They are too slow to fight germs
They would attack the body's own cells
check.why: A T cell attacks whatever their receptor fits. If the receptor fits a body protein, the T cell would attack the body, which is an autoimmune disease. So those T cells are removed before they leave the thymus.

flow.context: This is the last step of Thymus School. Here you add up the score and link the game to autoimmune disease and regulatory T cells.

projects.title: Hugs Are Safe: a true-or-false poster about how HIV spreads
projects.context: This project is about what people believe about HIV. On the first day you ask three grown-ups six true-or-false questions and count their answers. On the second day you make a poster that gives the right answer to each, with the reason. Many people still fear the wrong things, and that fear hurts people who live with HIV.

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
a large sheet of chart paper, or the back of an old calendar
sketch pens or crayons
three grown-ups to ask, at home or on the phone

projects.safety: Ask only grown-ups you know well. Nobody has to say whether they know a person with HIV, and you should not ask.

schedule.what: Write six true-or-false statements about HIV. Ask three grown-ups, and tally their answers.
Make a poster that gives the right answer and the reason for each statement. Put it up at home and show it to the people you asked.

projects.record: Keep the tally table of answers in your notebook. Write which statement the most people got wrong. Take a photograph of the finished poster.

setup.art: A notebook page with six numbered statements and three columns of ticks and crosses, one column for each grown-up asked.
setup.caption: 1. Day 1: ask three grown-ups six true-or-false questions and tally the answers.

setup.art: A child drawing a large poster on chart paper with two halves: one half showing a hug, a shared plate, a mosquito and a cough each with a green tick, the other half showing a drop of blood and a mother with a baby.
setup.caption: 2. Day 2: make a poster with the right answers and the reasons.

setup.art: The finished poster stuck on a wall beside a doorway, with a grandmother reading it.
setup.caption: 3. Put the poster up and show it to the people you asked.

flow.do: 1. Your child copies the six statements from the parent note. 2. Your child asks three grown-ups to answer true or false to each. 3. Tally the answers in a table. 4. Do not tell anyone the right answers yet.
flow.say: Ask each person all six. Write a tick for true and a cross for false. Do not tell them the answers yet. Which one do you think most people will get wrong? Why?
flow.kid: Copy the six statements. Ask three grown-ups: true or false? Tally their answers. Do not tell them the answers yet.
flow.parent: The six statements, with answers. 1. You can catch HIV by sharing a plate or a tumbler. False. 2. A mosquito can carry HIV from one person to another. False. 3. You can catch HIV by hugging or shaking hands. False. 4. HIV can pass through blood, for example on a reused needle. True. 5. A mother with HIV can pass the virus to her baby if she gets no treatment. True. 6. A person with HIV who takes medicine every day can live a long and healthy life. True.
flow.context: This is day 1 of Hugs Are Safe. Here you ask three grown-ups six true-or-false questions about HIV and tally their answers.

flow.do: 1. Look at the tally together and find the statement most people got wrong. 2. Your child plans the poster in pencil. 3. One side shows how HIV does not spread. 4. The other side shows how it does. 5. Add one reason beside each.
flow.say: Which statement fooled the most people? Put that one biggest on your poster. For each one, write the reason, so that people can check it and need not just believe you.
flow.kid: Find the statement most people got wrong. Plan your poster. Show how HIV does not spread, and how HIV does. Write a reason for each.
flow.parent: Reasons a child can write: HIV breaks down quickly outside the body. HIV does not pass through healthy skin. A mosquito injects saliva, not the last person's blood. Hospitals use a new needle each time. Medicine for the mother protects the baby. HIV also passes in sex between grown-ups, and your child can write that plainly.
flow.context: This is the first part of day 2 of Hugs Are Safe. Here you plan and draw the poster, with a reason beside each statement.

flow.do: 1. Put the poster up at home. 2. Your child shows it to each person who answered. 3. Ask each person whether anything surprised them. 4. Your child writes down what they said.
flow.say: Show your poster to everyone you asked. Did anything surprise them? Did anyone change their mind? What changed it?
flow.kid: Put up your poster. Show it to the people you asked. Ask what surprised them. Write down what they say.
flow.think: If nobody has ever caught HIV from a hug, where does the fear of a hug come from?
flow.context: This is the last part of Hugs Are Safe. Here you show the poster to the people you asked and find out whether it changed anyone's mind.

challenges.title: The Allergy-Safe Party: one table that six friends can all eat from
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about food allergies and coeliac disease. Six friends are coming to a party, and four of them must each avoid one food. You plan a table of snacks so that every child can eat well and nobody is left out.
challenges.problem: Plan five snacks and one drink for six children. One child is allergic to peanuts, one to milk and one to egg. One has coeliac disease and cannot eat wheat, barley or rye. Every child must be able to eat at least four of the six things.
constraints: Every child must be able to eat at least four of the six things on the table.
At least two things must be safe for all six children.
Each dish needs a small card that says what it contains.
Use foods you can make or buy near your home.
materials: paper and a pencil for the menu
small pieces of card for the labels
the packets in your kitchen, to check their labels
a grown-up who cooks, to ask what goes into each dish
general: Choose dishes that are free of all four foods to begin with, such as idli with coconut chutney, sundal, fruit and lemon juice.
Check every dish for hidden ingredients by asking the cook and reading the packets.
Give each dish its own spoon, so that no food is carried from one dish to another.
creative: Hunt for hidden wheat and milk. Rava is wheat. Ghee, paneer, curd and khoa are milk. Powdered hing is often mixed with wheat flour, so read the packet.
Put a small coloured flag in each dish, with one colour for each of the four foods, so that a child can see at a glance what to avoid.
Ask the four friends or their parents before the party what they like to eat. They know their own allergy best.
challenges.your_turn: Now write your own menu. Make a table with the six things down the side and the six children along the top, and tick who can eat what. Does every child have at least four ticks?

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a table drawn on it: six dishes listed down the side and six children's names along the top, with ticks and crosses being filled in by a child.
setup.caption: 1. List the dishes and the children in a table. Tick who can eat what.

setup.art: A low table set for a party with idlis, a bowl of sundal, cut fruit, murukku and tumblers of lemon juice, each dish with its own spoon and a small folded label card.
setup.caption: 2. Give each dish a label card and its own spoon.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem aloud. 2. Your child lists ten party snacks they like. 3. For each, ask a cook or read a packet to find out whether it holds peanuts, milk, egg or wheat. 4. Cross out or mark each one.
flow.say: First list the snacks you would love at a party. Then we become detectives. What is really inside each one? How can we find out?
flow.kid: List ten party snacks. Find out what is in each one. Ask a cook or read the packet. Mark peanuts, milk, egg and wheat.
flow.parent: Common surprises: kesari and upma are made of rava, which is wheat. Payasam, laddus made with ghee and most chocolates hold milk. Cake holds wheat, milk and egg. Many namkeen mixtures hold peanuts.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Allergy-Safe Party. Here you list party snacks and find out what each one really contains.

flow.do: 1. Your child chooses five snacks and one drink. 2. Draw the table of dishes and children. 3. Tick who can eat what. 4. Check the two rules: four ticks for every child, and two dishes safe for all. 5. Change the menu until both rules are met.
flow.say: Choose your six things and fill in the table. Does every child have four ticks? Are two dishes safe for everyone? If not, what will you swap?
flow.kid: Choose five snacks and one drink. Draw the table. Tick who can eat what. Check both rules. Swap dishes until the rules are met.
flow.parent: A menu that works: idli with coconut chutney, chana sundal, cut fruit, rice murukku, banana chips and lemon juice. Ask what oil the murukku and chips were fried in, because some families with a peanut allergy also avoid groundnut oil.
flow.context: This step of the Allergy-Safe Party chooses the menu and checks every child against every dish.

flow.do: 1. Your child writes a label card for each dish. 2. Ask how to stop food moving from one dish to another. 3. Ask the question below. 4. Your child improves the plan once more.
flow.say: Your menu is safe on paper. What could still go wrong at the real table? How will you stop it? And how will the four friends feel at your party?
flow.kid: Write a label for each dish. Think what could go wrong at the table. Fix your plan. How will your friends feel?
flow.think: A child with an allergy reads labels and asks questions at every meal. What could the rest of us do to make that easier?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Allergy-Safe Party. Here you label the dishes and think about what could still go wrong at the table.

challenges.title: Fewer Tests: find one positive sample among eight
challenges.context: This is a puzzle that real laboratories face. A grown-up hides a pinch of washing powder in one of eight cups of water. Turmeric water is your test, as in the Titre Test, and it turns red with washing powder. Testing every cup takes eight tests. Your job is to find the cup with fewer.
challenges.problem: Eight cups of water look the same. One holds a pinch of washing powder. Find which one, using as few turmeric tests as you can. Eight tests is easy. Can you do it in four, or in three?
constraints: One test means one katori with one teaspoon of turmeric water added.
You may put spoonfuls from several cups into the same katori before you test it.
Never pour anything back into a cup, and rinse the spoon after every cup.
Write down your plan before you test.
materials: 8 cups, tumblers or katoris of water, numbered 1 to 8
a pinch of washing powder, hidden in one cup by a grown-up
half a tumbler of turmeric water, made as in the Titre Test
4 small katoris for testing, a teaspoon and a mug of rinse water
general: Test the cups one at a time. This always works, and it can take up to eight tests.
Mix a spoonful from each of cups 1 to 4 in one katori and test it. One test tells you which half holds the powder.
Keep halving: test two of the four, then one of the two. That finds the cup in three tests.
creative: Plan three mixtures before you test anything, so that every cup is in a different set of mixtures. Then the pattern of red and yellow names the cup, with all three tests run side by side.
Ask what happens if two cups hold powder. Work out a plan that still finds both.
Mixing makes each sample weaker. Use the Titre Test to check how many cups you can mix before the turmeric stops turning red.
challenges.your_turn: Now ask the grown-up to hide the powder in one of sixteen cups, or draw sixteen cups on paper. How many tests do you need? What is the pattern as the number of cups doubles?

setup.art: Eight numbered steel tumblers of clear water in a row on a counter, with a tumbler of yellow turmeric water, a teaspoon and four small katoris in front of them.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up hides a pinch of washing powder in one of eight cups.

setup.art: A child putting one teaspoon from each of the first four tumblers into one katori, which has turned red after turmeric water was added.
setup.caption: 2. Mix a spoonful from several cups in one katori and test the mixture. Red means the powder is in one of those cups.

flow.do: 1. Number eight cups and fill each with the same amount of water. 2. Send your child out, and stir a good pinch of washing powder into one cup. 3. Read the problem and the rules aloud. 4. Ask for a plan on paper.
flow.say: One of these eight cups holds washing powder. You could test all eight. Can you think of a way to learn about several cups with one test? Write your plan.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to hide washing powder in one of eight cups. Read the rules. Write a plan to find it with few tests.
flow.parent: Use a bigger pinch than in the Titre Test, because mixing with three other cups makes the sample four times weaker. Check that a spoonful from the powder cup, mixed with three spoonfuls of plain water, still turns turmeric red.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fewer Tests. Here a grown-up hides washing powder in one of eight cups, and you plan how to find it.

flow.do: 1. Your child carries out the plan. 2. Count every test. 3. Rinse the spoon after every cup. 4. When the cup is found, check it with one last test.
flow.say: Carry out your plan and count your tests. Before each test, tell me what a red result would mean and what a yellow result would mean.
flow.kid: Follow your plan. Count each test. Rinse the spoon every time. Before each test, say what red and yellow would mean.
flow.parent: Halving finds the cup in three tests. If your child tests one cup at a time, let them finish, then ask whether one test could tell them about four cups at once.
flow.context: This step of Fewer Tests carries out your plan and counts how many turmeric tests you used.

flow.do: 1. Compare the number of tests with eight. 2. Ask how many tests sixteen cups would need. 3. Tell the true story in the parent note. 4. Your child writes the pattern.
flow.say: You found one cup in eight with a few tests. How many would you need for sixteen cups? For thirty-two? What is the pattern?
flow.kid: How many tests did you use? Work out how many you would need for 16 cups. Then for 32. Write the pattern.
flow.parent: Each time the number of cups doubles, halving needs only one more test: 8 cups need 3 tests, 16 need 4 and 32 need 5. The economist Robert Dorfman suggested mixing blood samples in 1943, to test American soldiers for an infection with fewer tests. In 2020, laboratories in India mixed five samples at a time to test for the coronavirus when test kits were short. It works well only when few people are infected.
flow.context: This is the last step of Fewer Tests. Here you find the pattern in the number of tests and hear how real laboratories use the same idea.

worksheets.title: Antibodies, the body's record and the defence gone wrong (core)

items.p: What shape is an antibody?
opts: Like the letter Y
Like a ball
Like a long thread
items.why: An antibody is a Y-shaped protein. The two tips of the Y fit the antigen, and the stem tells other cells what to do.

items.p: The two tips of an antibody fit one ____, which is usually a molecule on the outside of a germ.
items.why: An antigen is any molecule the immune system can recognise by its shape. Each antibody fits one antigen.

items.p: What do antibodies do to a germ?
opts: Burn the germ with acid
Swallow the germ
Stick to germs and flag them
items.why: Antibodies stick. They block germs, clump them and flag them for phagocytes. Choosing 'swallow' mixes up antibodies with phagocytes, who are whole cells.

items.p: True or false: antibodies kill germs all by themselves.
items.why: False. An antibody only holds on. Phagocytes and complement proteins destroy the germs that antibodies have flagged.

items.p: Match each cell to the job that cell does.
pairs: waits for the germ to return
items.why: Each kind of immune cell has a different job, and they work together.

items.p: Put these in order, for a first infection.
a: A germ gets into the body
A B cell's antibody fits the germ's antigen
The B cell divides into many cells
items.why: The fit comes first. Then the chosen B cell multiplies, and the new cells become antibody factories and memory cells.

items.p: A blood sample still tests positive when 64 times weaker, but not at 256. What is its titre?
items.why: The titre is the weakest dilution that still tests positive, so it is 64. Choosing 256 picks the first step where the test failed.

items.p: The time when a new infection is not yet found by an antibody test is called the ____ period.
items.why: In the window period the germ is in the body, but the body has not yet made enough antibody for the test to find.

items.p: True or false: an allergy is the immune system answering something harmless.
items.why: True. Pollen, dust mites and peanut protein do no harm themselves. The body's answer causes the trouble.

items.p: Is each of these an allergy or an autoimmune disease?
items.why: In an allergy the target is a harmless thing from outside. In an autoimmune disease the target is part of the person's own body.

items.p: Which cells does HIV infect and destroy?
opts: Red blood cells
Helper T cells
Skin cells
items.why: HIV fits a molecule called CD4 on helper T cells. These cells switch the rest of the defence on, so losing them weakens everything.

items.p: Which of these can pass HIV from one person to another?
opts: A mosquito bite
Sharing a tumbler
A reused injection needle
items.why: HIV passes in blood, so a reused needle can carry the virus. HIV does not pass through shared tumblers or mosquitoes.

items.p: One antibody lasts only weeks. Explain how a person still has measles antibodies fifty years after measles.
items.a: Some plasma cells live in the bone marrow for many years. They keep making fresh measles antibodies all the time, to replace the ones that are broken down.
items.why: A strong answer says that long-lived plasma cells keep making new antibodies. The antibodies themselves are not fifty years old.

items.p: Draw one antibody holding two germs. Label the two tips and the stem.
items.a: A Y shape with one germ at each tip. The tips are labelled as the parts that fit the antigen. The stem is labelled as the part that phagocytes grip.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that both tips are the same and that one antibody can join two germs.

items.p: After a bee sting, a friend's throat swells and she struggles to breathe. What must happen at once?
items.a: This is anaphylaxis, which is an emergency. A grown-up must be told at once. She needs an adrenaline injection if she carries one, and an ambulance to hospital. In India, call 108 or 112.
items.why: A strong answer names it as an emergency and says adrenaline and hospital. Waiting to see if it passes is dangerous.

worksheets.title: Classes of antibody, the thymus and HIV (stretch)

items.p: Why does an antibody have two matching tips?
opts: To fit two different kinds of germ
To cut a germ in half
To hold two germs, or one germ twice
items.why: Two matching tips let one antibody join two germs into a clump, or grip one germ firmly in two places. The tips are the same, so they fit the same antigen.

items.p: True or false: a B cell can keep the same antibody tips and change the stem.
items.why: True. The tips decide what the antibody fits. The stem decides where it goes and what happens next. Changing the stem turns IgM into IgG, IgA or IgE with the same fit.

items.p: Match each class of antibody to where it is found or when it is made.
pairs: made first in a new infection
in tears, spit and mother's milk
items.why: The stem of each class sends the antibody to a different place and gives it a different job.

items.p: Put the steps of an allergy in order.
a: The body meets the allergen for the first time
B cells make IgE that fits the allergen
The IgE settles on mast cells
The allergen comes again and links two IgE antibodies
items.why: An allergy needs two meetings. The first prepares the mast cells. The second sets them off.

items.p: What does histamine do to small blood vessels?
opts: Makes them wider and leaky
Makes them narrower
Blocks them completely
items.why: Histamine widens small blood vessels and makes them leaky, so fluid moves into the skin or the nose lining. That gives redness, swelling and a runny nose.

items.p: Young T cells are tested in the ____, a soft organ behind the breastbone.
items.why: The thymus shows young T cells samples of the body's own proteins and removes the T cells who would attack them.

items.p: What happens in the thymus to a young T cell whose receptor fits a body protein strongly?
opts: That T cell becomes a B cell
That T cell is removed
That T cell is copied many times
items.why: A T cell who fits the body would attack the body, so the thymus gives that cell a signal to die. Choosing 'copied' is what happens later to a T cell who fits a germ.

items.p: Can HIV pass from one person to another in this way?
items: from a mother to her baby, with no treatment
items.why: HIV passes in blood, in sex between grown-ups, and from mother to baby. The virus does not pass through skin, food, air or mosquitoes.

items.p: A person's HIV antibody test is negative. Give one reason why the person could still have HIV.
items.a: The person may have caught HIV only a few weeks ago. The body has not yet made enough antibodies for the test to find. This is the window period, so the test is done again later.
items.why: A strong answer says that the test looks for antibodies and that antibodies take weeks to appear.

items.p: In Boston, 6 inoculated people died and 844 others died. Why is that comparison unfair as it stands?
items.a: The two groups were very different in size. Only 247 people were inoculated, and 5,759 caught smallpox the usual way. We must compare how many died out of every 100 in each group.
items.why: A strong answer says that counts from groups of different sizes cannot be compared directly, and that a rate is needed.

items.p: True or false: HIV medicines remove every virus from the body.
items.why: False. The medicines stop HIV from copying. HIV DNA stays hidden inside resting cells, so the virus returns if the medicines are stopped.

items.p: Why are three HIV medicines given together?
opts: Each one treats a different illness
One tablet is too small to work
A virus resisting all three is very unlikely
items.why: HIV changes fast, so a virus who resists one medicine soon appears. A virus who resists three different medicines at once is very unlikely.

items.p: Sketch a line graph of helper T cells over ten years of HIV. Add a second line with medicine.
items.a: The first line falls slowly from a high start towards a low level over about ten years. The second line falls at first, then rises again from the year the medicine starts.
items.why: A strong sketch shows a slow fall over years, not a sudden drop, and shows that medicine lets the count recover.

items.p: Two views about what an allergy is.

views.who: A doctor in an allergy clinic
views.says: An allergy is an error. Pollen and peanuts are harmless, and the reaction only does harm.

views.who: A scientist who studied bee venom in mice
views.says: Mice who had made IgE against venom survived a bigger dose. The reaction is a real defence against poisons, aimed at the wrong things today.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with more? Give a reason from this lesson.
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side and gives evidence. For the scientist: the mouse studies, and the way sneezing and vomiting push things out of the body. For the doctor: most allergens are not poisons, and the reaction can kill.
items.why: Both can be true together. A defence that once protected against venoms can still be an error when it fires at peanuts.

items.p: Why was cowpox a safer way to protect people than smallpox inoculation?
opts: Cowpox is a mild disease in humans
Cowpox viruses have no antigens
Cows never fall ill
items.why: Cowpox virus is closely related to smallpox virus, so antibodies against one fit the other. But cowpox is mild in humans, so nobody died of the protection. Inoculation used real smallpox, and a few people died of it.

items.p: How does the tip of an antibody hold an antigen?
opts: By tiny hooks that pierce it
By many weak attractions between atoms
By one strong chemical bond
items.why: Many weak attractions act together where the shapes and electric charges match. No strong bond forms, which is why a close fit matters and why the antibody can let go.

items.p: Explain why a molecule of slightly the wrong shape does not stay on an antibody's tip.
items.a: The wrong shape touches the tip at only a few points. A few weak attractions are not enough to hold against the moving water around them, so the molecule drifts away.
items.why: A strong answer says that the hold comes from many weak attractions together, and that a poor fit gives too few of them.

items.p: True or false: a high titre means that a sample holds a lot of antibody.
items.why: True. A sample with a lot of antibody can be made much weaker and still test positive, so its titre is a large number.

items.p: Put these five samples in order, from the most antibody to the least.
items.why: The larger the titre, the more times the sample was weakened before the test stopped seeing it, so the more antibody it held.

items.p: One test looks for a germ's genes, not for antibodies. Why can it find a new infection sooner?
opts: Genes are bigger than antibodies
Antibodies hide from tests
The germ is there before the antibodies
items.why: The germ is in the body from the first day. Antibodies appear only after the body has had weeks to answer. A test for the germ's genes has a shorter window period.

items.p: The thymus removes T cells who fit the body. Give one reason why autoimmune disease still happens.
items.a: The test in the thymus is not perfect, and some T cells who fit the body slip through. Regulatory T cells usually calm them, but this can fail. Also, a germ's antigen can look like a body protein, so the answer to the germ hits the body too.
items.why: A strong answer gives one of these: an imperfect test, a failure of regulatory T cells, or a germ that resembles a body part.

items.p: Which idea about allergies does each finding support?
items: mice with IgE against bee venom survived a bigger dose
babies who ate peanut early had fewer peanut allergies
sneezing and vomiting push a poison out of the body
babies with sore, broken skin more often become allergic to foods
items.why: Evidence about venoms and getting poisons out supports the toxin idea. Evidence about how a baby first meets a food supports the early food idea. Both ideas can be true.

items.p: After a throat infection, antibodies against the bacterium also damage the heart. What is the best explanation?
opts: Part of the bacterium resembles a heart protein
The bacterium is living in the heart
The antibodies have grown too old
items.why: An antibody sticks to whatever its tips fit. If a heart protein has nearly the same shape as a bacterial antigen, the same antibody sticks to both. This happens in rheumatic fever.

items.p: HIV copies their genes with many mistakes. Explain how this helps the virus escape antibodies.
items.a: The mistakes change the shape of the virus's antigens a little each time. Antibodies made against the old shape fit the new shape poorly. By the time the body makes new antibodies, the virus has changed again.
items.why: A strong answer links copying mistakes to changed shapes, and changed shapes to antibodies that no longer fit.

items.p: Two views about who should get the credit for stopping smallpox.

views.says: Edward Jenner. He tested cowpox, published his results and gave the world a safe vaccine.

views.who: A historian of Africa and Asia
views.says: The healers of West Africa, India and China, and Onesimus. They knew that a small dose protects, long before Jenner.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with more? Give a reason from this lesson.
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side and gives evidence. For the historian: inoculation was used in Boston in 1721, and Jenner himself was inoculated as a boy. For the book: cowpox was far safer, and Jenner tested it and wrote it down so that others could check.
items.why: Both did something real. The first group found that protection is possible. Jenner found a much safer way and tested it openly.

items.p: T cells who calm other immune cells down are called ____ T cells.
items.why: Regulatory T cells are a second guard outside the thymus. They hold back T cells who would attack the body.

items.p: 15 of 100 untreated people died, and 2 of 100 treated people. What must you check before saying the treatment worked?
items.a: Check whether the two groups were alike to begin with. The treated people may have been healthier, richer or better cared for. Also check that the treated group was large enough for the result not to be chance.
items.why: A strong answer says that the groups must be alike in every way except the treatment before the difference can be put down to the treatment.

items.p: Draw a mast cell before and after an allergen links two IgE antibodies. Label IgE, allergen and histamine.
items.a: Before: a round cell full of dots, with Y shapes standing on the surface. After: one allergen touching the tips of two Y shapes, and dots leaving the cell. The Y shapes are labelled IgE and the dots are labelled histamine.
items.why: A strong drawing shows one allergen joining two IgE antibodies, because that link is what sets the mast cell off.

items.p: One of eight samples is positive. You mix four and test the mixture. What does the result tell you?
opts: Nothing useful at all
Which half holds the positive sample
Exactly which sample is positive
items.why: If the mixture is positive, the positive sample is one of those four. If it is negative, it is one of the other four. One test has halved the search.

items.p: True or false: a person whose HIV is too low to measure does not pass HIV on through sex.
items.why: True. Studies of thousands of couples found no case of HIV passing from a partner whose virus was too low to measure. People say 'undetectable equals untransmittable'.

quiz.p: Which part of an antibody fits the antigen?
opts: The stem of the Y
The whole surface
The two tips of the Y
quiz.why: The two tips fit the antigen. The stem is the part that phagocytes and mast cells hold. Choosing 'the stem' mixes up the two jobs.

quiz.p: Antibodies tie many germs into one lump. Why does that help the body?
opts: A lump cannot spread, and is swallowed whole
A lump is squeezed until the germs die
A lump turns into more antibodies
quiz.why: Clumped germs cannot spread through the body, and one phagocyte can swallow the whole clump. Antibodies do not squeeze or kill.

quiz.p: Which cells keep releasing antibodies for years after an infection is over?
opts: Mast cells in the skin
Plasma cells in the bone marrow
Red blood cells
quiz.why: Long-lived plasma cells in the bone marrow keep making fresh antibodies. Mast cells hold IgE on their surface but do not make antibodies.

quiz.p: What does an antibody test look for in a person's blood?
opts: The living germ
Damaged red blood cells
Antibodies the body made against the germ
quiz.why: The test finds the body's answer to the germ. That is why it can show an infection from long ago, and why it can miss one from last week.

quiz.p: True or false: a negative antibody test always means that the person has no infection.
quiz.why: False. In the first weeks the body has not yet made enough antibody to find. This is the window period, so the test is repeated later.

quiz.p: Which class of antibody sits on mast cells and causes allergies?
opts: IgE
IgG
IgA
quiz.why: IgE fixes its stem to mast cells. IgG is the main antibody in blood, and IgA is in tears, spit and milk.

quiz.p: Why does a baby's first mosquito bite usually leave no bump?
opts: Babies have no mast cells
The baby has no IgE against saliva yet
Mosquito saliva cannot enter a baby's skin
quiz.why: A bump is the body's answer to mosquito saliva, and it needs IgE made after an earlier bite. At the first bite there is none yet.

quiz.p: In an autoimmune disease, what does the immune system attack?
opts: A harmless food or pollen
A virus hiding in the body
Part of the person's own body
quiz.why: 'Auto' means self. The defence attacks the person's own cells, such as the insulin-making cells in type 1 diabetes. Choosing 'a harmless food' describes an allergy.

quiz.p: How do antiretroviral medicines help a person with HIV?
opts: They stop the virus from copying
They remove every virus in a week
They are helper T cells in a tablet
quiz.why: The medicines stop HIV from copying, so helper T cells are no longer destroyed and the body makes more. The virus stays hidden, so the medicines are taken for life.

quiz.p: True or false: you can catch HIV by sharing a tiffin box with a friend who has HIV.
quiz.why: False. HIV passes in blood, in sex between grown-ups and from a mother to her baby. The virus does not pass through food, plates, touch or air.

quiz.p: Why did a small dose of smallpox in a scratch protect a person for life?
opts: The dose used up all the smallpox nearby
The body kept memory cells and antibodies
The scratch let the illness out
quiz.why: The body answered the small dose and kept plasma cells and memory cells against smallpox. The healers who did this did not know about these cells, but they knew that it worked.

quiz.p: 844 of 5,759 people died in one group, and 6 of 247 in another. What is the fair comparison?
opts: The two numbers of deaths
The two sizes of the groups
Deaths out of every 100 in each group
quiz.why: The groups are very different in size, so the counts cannot be compared directly. Working out deaths in every 100 gives about 15 and about 2.

applications: Blood banks in India test every lesson of donated blood for HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C before anyone receives it.
Rapid test strips for dengue, malaria and pregnancy have antibodies fixed to the paper. A line appears where the antibodies catch what the test is looking for.
Before a blood transfusion, a laboratory mixes a drop of blood with antibodies. If the red cells clump, the blood group is known.

Snake antivenom is made of antibodies. Horses are given tiny, safe doses of venom, and the antibodies from their blood are given to people who have been bitten. Irula snake catchers near Chennai collect much of the venom used in India.
Many new medicines for cancers and autoimmune diseases are antibodies made in factories. Their names often end in 'mab'.
A person who has a new kidney or heart takes medicines that calm T cells, so that the body does not attack the new organ.
People with severe allergies carry an adrenaline injector pen, and food packets print the allergens they contain.
A pregnant woman with HIV takes antiretroviral medicines, and her baby is very likely to be born without the virus.

open_questions.q: Can anyone make a vaccine that protects against HIV?
open_questions.why_open: HIV changes shape faster than any vaccine made so far can follow, and hides inside cells. Large trials over forty years have not given good protection. Scientists are now trying to guide the body, step by step, towards rare antibodies that fit the parts of HIV that cannot change.

open_questions.q: Why are about four out of five people with autoimmune diseases women?
open_questions.why_open: Hormones, genes on the X chromosome and pregnancy have all been suggested, and each has some evidence. Nobody knows how much each one matters.

open_questions.q: Why have allergies become so much more common in the last sixty years?
open_questions.why_open: Genes cannot change that fast. Fewer microbes in early life, changes in food, cleaner water, more time indoors and air pollution are all being studied. No single cause explains the rise everywhere.

open_questions.q: How do some plasma cells stay alive for a whole human lifetime?
open_questions.why_open: Most cells who work that hard die within weeks. Long-lived plasma cells sit in special places in the bone marrow and get signals from the cells around them. What exactly keeps them alive is not yet clear.

open_questions.q: Can a body that has started attacking itself be taught tolerance again?
open_questions.why_open: Doctors can calm the whole immune system, but that leaves a person open to infections. Scientists are testing ways to switch off the attack on one target only, for example by growing more regulatory T cells. It works in some animals and is only beginning in people.

open_questions.q: Can HIV be cured in everyone who has it?
open_questions.why_open: A few people have been cured after a risky bone marrow transplant for cancer. The virus's DNA hides in resting cells where no medicine reaches. Nobody yet knows a safe way to find and clear every one of those cells.

ask_kids: A mosquito bit you an hour ago and the bump is still there. Who made that bump?
Which germs do you think your blood remembers? How could a doctor find out?
You look at this packet. Who needs to read the 'Contains' line every single time?
Your friend cannot eat wheat. What on this table can she eat?
If a test says no, does that always mean no? When might it be wrong?
Would you share your tiffin with a friend who has HIV? What is your reason?
Is a stronger immune system always a better one? What could go wrong?
What is the oldest thing your body remembers that your mind does not?

jokes.j: What is an antibody's favourite letter?
jokes.a: Y. And no one ever asks why.

jokes.j: Why do antibodies make good friends?
Why are memory cells no fun at a surprise party?
jokes.a: They have seen it all before.

jokes.j: What did the mast cell say to the pollen grain?
jokes.a: You make me want to burst.

jokes.j: Why did the turmeric go red?
Why did the young T cell fail the test in the thymus?
What did the plasma cell say about taking a holiday?
jokes.a: I can't. I have thousands to make every second.

jokes.j: Why was the phagocyte pleased with the antibodies?
jokes.a: They had packed lunch into one lump.

jokes.j: Why did the baby's first mosquito bite not itch?
jokes.a: Her body and the mosquito had not been introduced.

maths.problem: In the Titre Test, each katori is 4 times weaker than the one before. How many times weaker than the first katori is the fifth? What fraction of the first katori's strength is that?
maths.answer: 256 times weaker. That is one part in 256 of the first katori's strength.
maths.explain: There are four steps from the first katori to the fifth, and each step makes the liquid 4 times weaker. 4 × 4 = 16. 16 × 4 = 64. 64 × 4 = 256. So the fifth katori has one 256th of the strength.
maths.context: This is about the Titre Test, where you move one spoon of sample into three spoons of water, again and again, to make a row of five katoris.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying by 4 again and again shows how a few simple steps reach a very weak sample. That is how a laboratory measures a large amount of antibody with five small bowls.

maths.problem: In Boston in 1721, 844 of the 5,759 people who caught smallpox died. Of the 247 people who were inoculated, 6 died. About how many died out of every 100 in each group? About how many times safer was inoculation?
maths.answer: About 15 in every 100, and about 2 in every 100. Inoculation was about 6 times safer.
maths.explain: 844 ÷ 5,759 = 0.147, which is about 15 in 100. 6 ÷ 247 = 0.024, which is about 2 in 100. Using the unrounded numbers, 14.7 ÷ 2.4 is about 6. The two counts of deaths, 844 and 6, cannot be compared directly because the groups are of very different sizes.
maths.context: This is about Boylston's Count, where you used the real numbers from the smallpox outbreak in Boston in 1721 to compare two groups of people.
maths.why_maths: A rate out of 100 lets you compare two groups of very different sizes fairly. Without it, the small group always looks safer just because it is small.

maths.problem: Half of the IgG antibodies in blood are broken down every 3 weeks. If no new ones were made, what fraction would be left after 12 weeks? A woman still has plenty of measles antibody 50 years after measles. What does that tell you?
maths.answer: One sixteenth would be left after 12 weeks. So her body must be making new measles antibodies all the time.
maths.explain: 12 weeks is 4 lots of 3 weeks, so the amount halves 4 times. 1 → one half → one quarter → one eighth → one sixteenth. After a year almost nothing would be left. Since she still has plenty after 50 years, plasma cells must be making fresh antibodies every day.
maths.context: This is about how the body keeps a record of a germ. One antibody lasts only weeks, yet a blood test finds antibodies many years later.
maths.why_maths: The halving pattern shows that old antibodies cannot explain a positive test after many years. The numbers force the conclusion that cells keep making new ones.

maths.problem: In Fewer Tests, halving finds one positive cup among 8 in 3 tests, and among 16 in 4 tests. How many tests are needed for 64 cups? Describe the pattern.
maths.answer: 6 tests. Each time the number of cups doubles, you need only one more test.
maths.explain: Each test cuts the cups left in half. 64 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1. That is 6 halvings, so 6 tests. Testing the cups one by one could take up to 64 tests.
maths.context: This is about the challenge Fewer Tests, where you mix spoonfuls from several cups in one katori and test the mixture with turmeric water.
maths.why_maths: Counting halvings shows why mixing samples saves so many tests when only a few people are infected. Laboratories used this to stretch scarce test kits.

maths.problem: In the Helper Count, a die takes out 3 and a half beans a year on average, and the body adds 2. You start with 20 beans. After about how many years will 4 beans be left? Why might your own run be different?
maths.answer: After about 11 years. Your run can be shorter or longer because each roll of the die is chance.
maths.explain: On average the katori loses 3.5 − 2 = 1.5 beans a year. To go from 20 beans to 4 beans it must lose 16. 16 ÷ 1.5 is a little under 11. A run of high rolls reaches 4 sooner, and a run of low rolls takes longer.
maths.context: This is about the Helper Count, the bean model in which beans stand for helper T cells and each roll of a die is one year with HIV.
maths.why_maths: An average rate lets you predict roughly how long the fall takes. Comparing the prediction with your run shows how chance spreads real results around the average.

maths.problem: Look at the made-up graph from the Red Line Test. At what time was the mark widest? How many minutes after the stroke had it shrunk to less than half of that width?
maths.answer: The mark was widest, at 9 mm, at 2 and 3 minutes. By 10 minutes it had shrunk to 1 mm, which is less than half of 9 mm.
maths.explain: Read the highest point of the line: 9 mm at 2 minutes and at 3 minutes. Half of 9 mm is 4.5 mm. At 5 minutes the mark is 6 mm, which is still more than half. At 10 minutes it is 1 mm. So it passed below half some time between 5 and 10 minutes.

roots.context: We have learned that blood holds antibodies against germs met long ago, and that a test can read them. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Titre Test, the turmeric never showed you a germ. It showed the washing powder, which stood for antibodies. Many real blood tests work the same way, and the germ may have gone years ago. So your blood holds a record of the germs you have met, and a stranger can read it.
deep_truth.habit: We think that the past is over, and that only a brain can keep a memory. But a body keeps what has happened to them in plasma cells and antibodies, for decades. A brain is one kind of hardware for memory, and cells keep memory too.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Titre Test you measured how much was in each sample without ever seeing it, only by a colour. In 1986, six women in Madras looked well, and their blood showed antibodies against HIV. People who lived through the flu of 1918 still carried B cells against that virus ninety years later.

three.who_am_i: Your blood holds answers to germs you met before you could talk. Part of who you are is everything your body has met and answered.
three.what_is_life: Every living being keeps some record of what has happened to them. A tree keeps rings, a bacterium keeps pieces of the genes of viruses who attacked, and you keep memory cells.
three.what_is_this_world: Things that have gone leave marks that stay. A test, a scar or a layer of rock lets us read what is no longer here.

roots.thread: A germ and a body look like two separate things. After they meet, the shape of the germ is kept inside the body as a matching antibody, and the body is changed for life. Part of your record came from your mother, whose antibodies crossed into you before you were born. A vaccine adds what people learned from illnesses long ago. So one drop of your blood holds marks left by many lives meeting.

science.text: The level of antibody against measles stays almost steady in a person's blood for decades after the infection or the vaccine.
Bacteria keep short pieces of the genes of viruses who attacked them, stored in their own DNA. Scientists call this store CRISPR. Bacteria use this store to recognise the same virus again.
Whether the immune system's memory and the brain's memory are the same kind of thing, or only share a word, is an open question.

other_view.view: Many scientists say that 'record' and 'memory' are words borrowed from human life. In their view, what stays in the blood is molecules and long-lived cells following chemistry, and it is not like recalling a birthday. The Buddha taught, in a different way, that there is no fixed self who owns a past. There is only a stream of changes, each one leading to the next.

practice.title: The small scar
practice.say: Find the small round scar high on your left arm. Most children in India have one, from a vaccine given soon after birth. If you cannot find one, rest a finger on your arm anyway. Close your eyes and breathe slowly five times. Your body met something here before you could talk. Your body still holds the answer today. What else might your body hold that your mind has forgotten? Open your eyes and tell me.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game and challenge in this lesson was reasoned through step by step as a family in a city flat would do it. None has yet been tried at home, so please treat times and amounts as a starting point. The Titre Test (in the core path) depends on your washing powder and your tap water. Turmeric turns red in alkaline water, and washing powder and washing soap are alkaline, but a bath soap or a liquid hand wash may be too mild. Check one spoonful first, as the first step says. If every katori turns red, use half a pinch. If only the first turns red, use more. Rinsing the spoon between katoris matters more than anything else. The Red Line Test is gentle and uses only a blunt spoon handle. Most people show a line that spreads and fades within fifteen minutes. On brown skin the mark may look darker and not red, so use light from the side. Some people show almost nothing, which the test treats as a real result. Peg Antibodies was checked by counting: seven double pegs join eight cards in a chain. The Helper Count loses one and a half beans a year on average, so most runs take 8 to 13 rolls. Boylston's Count and the maths were checked by arithmetic. Facts checked through web searches while writing: the Boston numbers of 1721, the Rose and Witebsky and the Roitt and Doniach papers of 1956, the discovery of IgE, the 2025 Nobel Prize, the antibody half-lives, the 1918 flu survivors, Cipla's price in 2001, the UNAIDS and NACO counts, and the title and channel of the three videos. The story of Sellappan Nirmala follows published accounts of her work. How she travelled to Vellore, and every conversation, are imagined, and the story's note says so. HIV is explained plainly, including that HIV passes in sex between grown-ups. Please read the explanation on living with HIV and preview the third video before sharing them with your child.
